Separation: nothing is being collected or completed; the reveal is a temporary x-ray window the child controls, and the SKILL is reading the hidden quantity exposed inside a body — a counting/cardinality act, not a picture-completion act. The hover-to-reveal-then-it-hides forces real looking.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: plush-animal outline + an inner dot-cluster layer + a translucent blue scanner rectangle + numeral tiles. CA5: warm vet-clinic, plush patients with cute faces, glowing x-ray skeleton/dot innards, Dr. Pip in a tiny coat.

designs.name: Footprint Detective
designs.mechanic: An animal walked across snow/mud leaving a TRAIL of clue tracks plus other evidence (a tuft of fur, a dropped acorn, a feather). The child follows/taps the trail of footprints in order to 'gather clues', and at the end deduces which of 3-4 suspect animals made them by matching attributes (this print has 4 toes + the fur is orange → the fox). They tap the deduced culprit.
designs.fun_no_competition: Playing detective; the 'aha' of clues adding up; a magnifying-glass cursor that enlarges each clue with a satisfying pop; the reveal of the culprit peeking out from behind a bush, caught (gently, smiling).
designs.character_world: Detective Mittens, a cat in a deerstalker hat with a magnifying glass, on the Case of the Missing Cookie.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — clues are tappable hotspots that flip open a fact card; suspects are 3-4 sprites; deduction = match accumulated attribute flags. Logic is simple state, no loop. Authoring the attribute sets is the real work.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is path-journey (move along a path) and match-pairs. Separation: the path here is a CLUE-GATHERING deduction trail, not a route to traverse for its own sake; the answer is DEDUCED by narrowing suspects from accumulated evidence, a logical-attribute reasoning act. No two clues alone solve it — the discovery is inferential.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: snowy scene + footprint trail + 3 clue icons + 4 suspect animal cards. CA5: storybook woodland mystery scene, Detective Mittens, glowing magnifier, animated 'caught!' reveal of the culprit.

designs.name: Fog-Lift Word Mountain
designs.mechanic: A target sight-word (or CVC word) sits behind thick fog. The child taps the matching picture/letter-sound choices one at a time; each CORRECT tap blows away one patch of fog, progressively REVEALING the hidden word underneath until it's fully readable — at which point the child reads it aloud (Hear-it confirms). Wrong taps puff a tiny harmless cloud, no penalty.
designs.fun_no_competition: Atmospheric suspense of fog lifting; the dreamy reveal of a mountaintop word; wind 'whoosh' sound and a sunrise breaking through when the word is fully clear.
designs.character_world: Nimbus, a little cloud-sheep who lives on Word Mountain and clears the sky for you.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — fog = overlay div with multiple semi-opaque patches removed on each correct answer (opacity/transform transitions); word text beneath revealed by removing patches. No loop.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is reveal-grid (correct answers uncover a picture tile-by-tile). Separation: what's revealed is a WORD being spelled into legibility, and the reveal is CONTINUOUS fog dissipation rather than discrete grid tiles, tied to letter-sound or sight-word matching. The discovery payoff is reading the word that emerges, an ELA act not a picture-puzzle.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: mountain bg + word text layer + 5-6 fog-patch PNGs + choice tiles. CA5: misty pastel mountain, Nimbus the cloud-sheep, layered drifting fog, golden sunrise reveal frame.

designs.name: Magnifier Spelling Bug Hunt
designs.mechanic: A leaf is covered in tiny camouflaged bugs, each bug carrying ONE letter on its back. The child is given a target word and drags a big magnifying lens over the leaf; only under the lens do the small letters become big and readable. They must find and tap the bug-letters IN ORDER to spell the word, the lens being the only way to read what each bug holds.
designs.fun_no_competition: Delight of zooming in to read a hidden letter; bugs that wiggle when magnified; the word filling in bug-by-bug at the bottom; a happy buzz when the word is complete.
designs.character_world: Lupe the ladybug, a tiny entomologist who hands you her magnifier.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — lens = draggable div with a CSS scale transform on a clipped region (or per-bug scale-up when under lens via proximity check); ordered-tap spelling = simple sequence state.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is i-spy-scene and magic-trace. Separation: the letters are too small to read until MAGNIFIED — the lens is a true reveal tool that changes legibility, and the task is ordered spelling (sequence) gated by a search-and-magnify discovery, not free scanning or tracing.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: leaf bg + scattered small bug sprites with letters + magnifier graphic. CA5: lush macro leaf world, charming letter-bugs, glass-lens distortion ring, Lupe with a tiny notebook.

designs.name: Sound Sonar (Hidden in the Deep)
designs.mechanic: Sea creatures hide in dark water. The child taps a sonar 'ping' button which sends a ripple; hidden creatures briefly flash their silhouette AND a sound plays (the spoken NAME of the creature, or its initial sound). The child must, by the audio cue + silhouette, identify and tap where the named-target creature is hiding before the ping fades — using sense/detection rather than sight.
designs.fun_no_competition: Submarine sonar suspense; the ping ripple and creature-flash; pairing a sound you hear to a shape you glimpse; gentle bubbles and a friendly creature surfacing to say hello when found.
designs.character_world: Captain Dot, a small submarine-driving otter exploring the Quiet Deep.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — ping = an expanding circle animation that briefly toggles opacity on hidden sprites + triggers an audio cue (LCSAudio); tap-to-find = hotspot check. Brief CSS-timed reveal, no loop.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is pop-the-right-ones and i-spy-scene. Separation: the things are INVISIBLE until pinged and the primary detection channel is AUDIO/echo (sense what you can't see), pairing a heard name/sound to a momentarily-revealed location — a listening+phoneme task driven by active sensing, not visual scanning.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: dark-water bg + hidden creature silhouettes + sonar button + sub. CA5: deep-sea blues, glowing sonar ripple, charming sea creatures (silhouette + lit forms), Captain Dot's porthole sub.

designs.name: Lift-the-Flap Math Story
designs.mechanic: A story scene shows e.g. '3 bunnies are visiting. Some are hiding under the bushes!' Several bushes/boxes are closed flaps. The child is told the WHOLE (5 bunnies total) and sees some (3 in the open); they tap flaps to peek under each, revealing how many are hidden, and must decide the missing PART (how many are hidden = 2) by tapping the numeral — combining seen + hidden to make the whole.
designs.fun_no_competition: Lift-the-flap surprise (classic board-book joy); the giggle of bunnies peeking out; figuring out the hidden number; flaps that bounce open with a soft pop.
designs.character_world: Burrow the bunny family in a meadow full of hiding spots.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — flaps = clickable divs with an open-state showing the hidden count; whole/part logic = simple arithmetic check; numeral choices tappable. No loop.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is reveal-grid and feed-the-friend. Separation: this is part-part-whole DECOMPOSITION driven by lifting flaps to discover the hidden addend — the reveal directly serves the math (hidden quantity = the unknown part). Discovery answers an addition/decomposition question, not a picture or a counting-only task.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: meadow + bushes/boxes as flaps + bunny sprites + numeral tiles. CA5: storybook meadow, lift-flap bushes with shadow underneath, peeking bunnies, soft pop-open animation.

designs.name: Color-Filter Lens Reveal
designs.mechanic: A page looks like meaningless colored noise/scribble. The child drags one of several colored filter lenses (red/blue/green) over it; ONLY the correct filter makes a hidden picture or word pop out of the camouflage (like a red-lens decoder). The task: read the prompt ('find the lens that reveals a CAT'), try lenses, and tap the picture once revealed — choosing the right tool to expose hidden info. Gate the reveal-then-identify on a phonics decision (e.g. identify the letter/word once exposed and name its sound), so it instantiates RF.K.1.b letter recognition instead of merely picking a filter.
designs.fun_no_competition: Secret-decoder-ring magic; the thrill when the right filter makes a hidden picture leap out of chaos; swapping lenses to see what each reveals; collecting decoded secrets in a spy notebook.
designs.character_world: Agent Acorn, a squirrel spy with a satchel of decoder lenses.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — filter = a tinted overlay + a hidden layer that becomes visible only under a matching CSS mix-blend/mask; lens drag swaps which hidden layer shows. CSS blend modes + masks; no loop.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is reveal-grid and sort-home. Separation: the reveal requires picking the RIGHT decoder tool (color filter) — a tool-selection-to-expose mechanic with secret-decoder delight; nothing is being completed or sorted. Distinct from the flashlight (continuous sweep) and x-ray (window) because here the discovery is choosing which lens unlocks the image.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: noise bg + per-color hidden image layers + 3 colored lens PNGs + spy notebook. CA5: spy-lab aesthetic, Agent Acorn, glossy decoder lenses, camouflage patterns that resolve into clean pictures.

designs.name: Dust-for-Prints Letter Match
designs.mechanic: An invisible fingerprint sits on a surface. The child 'dusts' (drag a brush back-and-forth) to gradually reveal a hidden UPPERCASE letter print. Once revealed, a line-up of lowercase 'suspects' appears and the child taps the lowercase letter that MATCHES the dusted uppercase print (case-matching) — the forensic dusting reveals the clue to be matched.
designs.fun_no_competition: CSI-for-kids fun of dusting a hidden print into view; brush-swish particles; the reveal of a glowing letter; matching it to its little partner and clipping the case to a board.
designs.character_world: Officer Whiskers, a forensic cat at the Letter Lab.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — dust reveal = brush drag accumulates over a masked canvas region exposing the letter (canvas alpha-clear or per-region opacity); match = tap lowercase tile. Canvas brushing is a known simple pattern.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is match-pairs and magic-trace. Separation: the thing-to-match is HIDDEN and must be uncovered by a brushing/dusting reveal gesture before matching is even possible; the forensic dust-for-prints metaphor and the upper/lower case-matching standard are distinct from any pair-flip or trace.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: surface bg + hidden uppercase-letter mask + lowercase tiles + brush. CA5: forensic lab desk, Officer Whiskers, glowing dusted prints, fingerprint-dust particles, evidence clipboard.

designs.name: Decoder Wheel Secret Message
designs.mechanic: A short message is shown in symbol-code; a hidden letter sits behind each symbol. The child turns a decoder wheel (drag-rotate) to line a symbol up with the alphabet ring, REVEALING which letter it stands for, then taps that letter to fill the message slot. Decoding symbol→letter across the word spells a real word that, once cracked, plays/animates (e.g. 'CAT' → a cat appears).
designs.fun_no_competition: Secret-agent cipher cracking; the click of the wheel turning and a symbol's letter snapping into view; cracking the whole message and watching it come to life; collecting decoded words in a codebook.
designs.character_world: Cipher the fox, a junior codebreaker with a brass decoder wheel.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — wheel = a rotatable div (transform rotate on drag, snap to letter positions); symbol→letter lookup reveals on alignment; tap to place. Rotation + snap is simple; no loop.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is color-filter (10) and magic-machine. Separation: the reveal is achieved by ROTATING a decoder wheel to map a symbol to its hidden letter — a cipher-cracking, letter-correspondence act (print/letter-sound) rather than picking a filter. The rotary decode-each-symbol-then-spell flow is its own core.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: decoder wheel (2 rings) + symbol message + letter slots + reveal animation. CA5: spy-desk, Cipher fox, ornate brass code wheel, glowing symbol-to-letter reveals, codebook.

designs.name: Riddle Reveal (Deduce the Mystery Word)
designs.mechanic: Three or four spoken/written riddle clues describe a hidden picture-word ('I have four legs. I say woof. I am a pet. What am I?'). Clues appear one at a time; after each, the child may guess by tapping one of 4-6 picture choices — narrowing as clues add. Wrong early guesses just dim that choice; the right answer celebrates and re-reads the clues that pointed to it.
designs.fun_no_competition: The building suspense of each new clue narrowing it down; the 'I know it!' moment of an early correct deduction; the answer character pops out happily and the clue-trail lights up showing the reasoning.
designs.interaction: tap a picture choice after any clue (more clues available on demand)
designs.character_world: A riddle-loving genie/sphinx who poses gentle picture-riddles and is delighted when you reason it out.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — riddles are data {clues[], answer, distractors}; TTS for clues; tap choices; dimming logic trivial.
designs.distinctiveness: Progressive clue-narrowing word deduction — instantiates vocabulary/category reasoning (using describing attributes to identify a word). Distinct from logic-deduction-12 (suspect among story characters) because here it's identifying a vocabulary concept from descriptive attributes, and distinct from i-spy (find a NAMED target) because the target is described by properties, never named.
designs.asset_idea: stub: clue text lines + picture choice grid. CA5: friendly genie/sphinx character, themed picture-word sets (animals/foods/objects) with attribute-rich art, clue-scroll, glowing clue-trail reveal.

designs.name: Treasure Map Clue Trail (Sequence)
designs.mechanic: A treasure map shows a start and several numbered/lettered stepping spots, but the route is hidden. The child reveals the path by following ordered CLUES: 'first the spot that starts with /m/', 'next the spot that comes after 2', etc. Each correct choice uncovers the next leg of the trail (a dotted line + footprint) until the whole route to the treasure is revealed and the chest opens.
designs.fun_no_competition: Pirate-treasure-map adventure; each clue uncovering a new dotted leg with a stamp of a footprint; the X-marks-the-spot chest bursting open with confetti at the end.
designs.character_world: Pip the parrot navigator and a friendly map that draws itself.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — clue sequence = ordered state; each correct tap reveals a path-segment (SVG line draw or sprite). Logic is straightforward sequence checking; no loop.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is path-journey. Separation: in path-journey you traverse a KNOWN path; here the path is HIDDEN and you DISCOVER/construct it by solving an ordered clue at each step (sequence + letter/number recognition). The reveal is the route itself emerging from correct deductions, not movement along a given track.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: parchment map + spot markers + dotted-line segments + chest. CA5: aged treasure map, Pip parrot, footprint stamps, animated dotted trail drawing in, treasure chest open frame.

designs.name: Detective's Clue Board
designs.mechanic: A row of animal characters each want one item; the child reads/hears 2-4 picture clues ('The cat does NOT want the ball', 'The dog wants something round') and taps which item belongs to which character, eliminating possibilities until each is uniquely assigned. A clue 'lights up' green as the placement satisfies it. Tie the assignment to a CCSS-bearing attribute set (sort by category/count, K.MD.B.3) so the logic-grid instantiates classification reasoning rather than touching it; otherwise it is a generic puzzle.
designs.fun_no_competition: The 'aha!' when the last clue snaps everything into place and all the characters cheer with their item; clue cards literally glow as you satisfy them so progress feels like real detective work.
designs.interaction: tap-then-tap (select item, tap character slot) or drag item to character
designs.character_world: A friendly detective owl with a magnifying glass helps a group of woodland friends figure out whose lost item is whose.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — clue evaluation is simple boolean logic over a small attribute table; DOM tiles + CSS glow states; TTS for clue read-aloud.
designs.distinctiveness: This is a true logic-grid / constraint-satisfaction-by-elimination engine — the answer is forced by AND-ing negative and positive clues, not by matching a picture to its pair. Closest neighbor is match-pairs (template) and sort-home: separation is that NO single clue gives the answer; the child must cross-reference clues and use process-of-elimination. Distinct from logic-deduction-08 (analogy) which is one-step pattern transfer, not multi-clue cross-referencing.
designs.asset_idea: stub: colored boxes for characters + item icons. CA5: owl detective with magnifying glass, 4-5 woodland-friend characters with distinct silhouettes, item set (ball/bone/hat/cup), green glowing clue-card frame.

designs.name: Sudoku Picture Path (Mini Constraint Grid)
designs.mechanic: A 4x4 picture-Sudoku where each row, column, and 2x2 box must contain one of each of four pictures. Pre-filled cells constrain the rest; tapping an empty cell shows only the four pictures and the child reasons which is forced. A cell that violates a constraint shows a soft red outline; a fully legal grid blooms. Anchor the pictures to a real attribute classification (shape category, 2.G.A.1) so the deduce-the-forced-value instantiates a standard rather than being pure puzzle logic.
designs.fun_no_competition: The pure logic-puzzle 'click' of deducing a forced cell; soft non-punitive constraint feedback keeps it calm; the finished grid lights up region by region in a satisfying cascade.
designs.interaction: tap empty cell → tap chosen picture
designs.character_world: An owl puzzle-keeper who tends a 'thinking garden' grid and is delighted by a perfectly-filled board.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — 4x4 Sudoku legality (row/col/box) is simple; pre-generated solvable boards as data; DOM grid.
designs.distinctiveness: Classic deductive constraint-satisfaction with the box constraint adding genuine cross-region deduction. Distinct from logic-deduction-02 (Latin square, rows+cols only) by the added 2x2-box constraint, which forces multi-constraint intersection reasoning — a meaningfully harder deduction shape for grade 2. Not in any template; the existing sudoku app is operator-tooling, not a premium reasoning game with this scaffolded reveal.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 4x4 grid + four picture tokens. CA5: owl puzzle-keeper, four themed picture tokens (fruits or animals), region-divider grid styling, cascade bloom for a solved board.

designs.name: Guess My Rule (Sorting Machine)
designs.mechanic: A two-bin sorting machine has already sorted several example items (e.g. apple→left, truck→right, banana→left, bus→right). The child must INFER the hidden rule, then sort 3-4 NEW items correctly. Getting them right reveals the rule label ('Things you can eat!'). The child can ask for one more example before committing. Make the confirming sort use a categorizable attribute (K.MD.B.3 classify into categories) so rule-induction instantiates the classification standard; surface the rule explicitly on confirm.
designs.fun_no_competition: The detective thrill of cracking the secret rule; the machine 'whirs' and the rule label flips up with a fanfare when the child proves they figured it out — the reward is being RIGHT about the hidden logic.
designs.interaction: drag new items to a bin; tap 'show me one more example'
designs.character_world: A quirky robot sorting-machine with googly eyes that 'has a secret rule' and is tickled when you guess it.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — rule is a stored attribute predicate; examples and test items pulled from vocab attribute tags; DOM bins.
designs.distinctiveness: The skill is rule-INDUCTION from examples, the inverse of sort-home. In sort-home the category is stated; here it is HIDDEN and must be deduced from worked examples. No template has the child infer the classifier. Distinct from logic-deduction-01 (given clues) — here the child generates the hypothesis themselves.
designs.asset_idea: stub: gray machine box, two bins. CA5: googly-eyed robot machine with two chutes, conveyor of mixed item icons (food/vehicles/animals), flip-up rule-label sign.

designs.name: True, False, or Why (Math Statement Court)
designs.mechanic: A character states a math claim shown with pictures ('3 + 2 = 4' with three apples plus two apples; or '5 is greater than 8'). The child judges TRUE or FALSE — and on FALSE, taps the picture/numeral that PROVES it (e.g. taps the extra apple, or taps which number is actually bigger). The proof-tap is required, so the child must reason about WHY, not just guess.
designs.fun_no_competition: Playing 'judge' is empowering for a 6-year-old; a wrong claim gets a silly buzzer and the proof spotlight, a true claim gets a gavel-bang of approval — the delight is catching the character's mistake.
designs.interaction: tap True/False, then tap the proving evidence
designs.character_world: A wise tortoise judge in a tiny wig presides over a 'math court' where playful characters make claims that may be true or sneaky-false.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — statements are data {expr, truthValue, evidenceTarget}; equality/comparison check is arithmetic; tap targets are DOM elements.
designs.distinctiveness: Two-stage truth-evaluation + justification — distinct from any choice-tap template because a binary guess isn't accepted; the child must locate the evidence. The 'why' tap instantiates reasoning about equality/comparison rather than computing an answer. No template does claim-falsification.
designs.asset_idea: stub: text statement + counter dots, two buttons. CA5: tortoise judge with gavel, witness-stand characters, picture-equation props (apple groups, big/small numerals), spotlight + buzzer/gavel effects.

designs.name: Which One Breaks the Rule (Odd-One-Out With a Reason)
designs.mechanic: Four items share a property except one. The child taps the odd one — THEN must tap WHICH attribute makes it odd from 2-3 reason-cards ('because it has no corners', 'because it is not red'). Both the odd item AND the correct reason must be selected; a wrong reason for the right item is gently corrected.
designs.fun_no_competition: The satisfying click of 'I found it AND I know why'; the odd item does a sheepish wiggle and the matching reason-card stamps with a checkmark — naming the reason out loud (TTS echoes it) feels like being clever.
designs.interaction: tap odd item, then tap the reason-card
designs.character_world: A puzzled penguin professor who points at the group and asks 'one of these is different... but can you tell me WHY?'
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — items carry attribute tags; odd-item and reason are precomputed data; two-step tap gating in plain JS.
designs.distinctiveness: Standard odd-one-out only asks WHICH; this requires articulating WHY via an explicit attribute, making the reasoning explicit and instantiating attribute-classification. Different from logic-deduction-04 (judging a claim's truth) and from sort-home (binning). The reason-card layer is the key separation from a plain choice-tap.
designs.asset_idea: stub: four shape/item tiles + reason text buttons. CA5: penguin professor with pointer, attribute-rich shape/object set (some with/without corners, varied colors), reason-cards with little icons (corner/color/size).

designs.name: Balance Scale Detective
designs.mechanic: A two-pan balance shows blocks; one pan tips. The child must deduce a relationship — e.g. 'the box is heavier than the ball' — and answer a question ('put the heaviest thing on the bottom shelf' or 'which is lightest?') or make the scale balance by adding the deduced number of unit-blocks. Transitive reasoning across two weighings ('A>B and B>C, so...'). Bind the chained-weighing deduction to a comparison-of-measurable-attribute outcome the child reports (order by weight, 1.MD.A.1 / K.MD.A.2), so it instantiates comparison rather than abstract transitivity puzzle.
designs.fun_no_competition: Watching the scale tip and settle is inherently delightful; the 'aha' of chaining two weighings to know the order without ever weighing A against C directly; a balanced scale gives a satisfying gentle chime and level wobble.
designs.interaction: drag objects/unit-blocks onto pans; tap to answer the ordering question
designs.character_world: A friendly mouse shopkeeper weighing mystery parcels who needs help figuring out which is heaviest.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — weights are data, tilt is CSS rotate driven by sum comparison; transitivity is precomputed for the question.
designs.distinctiveness: Transitive/comparative deduction from observed states — the child infers an ordering they were never directly told, then acts on it. No template uses a physics-state (tilt) as the clue source. Distinct from logic-deduction-04 (symbolic claims) because the evidence is the visual balance, and from comparison apps because two weighings must be CHAINED.
designs.asset_idea: stub: simple beam + two pans + numbered blocks. CA5: mouse shopkeeper, ornate balance scale with springy beam, parcel/object weights, unit cube blocks, chime + level-glow on balance.

designs.name: Finish the Analogy (Pair Logic)
designs.mechanic: An analogy is shown as two picture-pairs with the last slot empty: cat→kitten, dog→? . The child taps the item that completes the SAME relationship from 3-4 choices (puppy, not bone or cat). The relationship type varies (parent→baby, object→use, animal→home, big→small).
designs.fun_no_competition: The clean 'click' of seeing the hidden relationship — the completed analogy animates the pair connecting with a little zap, and a wise character nods 'you saw the connection!'
designs.interaction: tap the choice that completes the analogy
designs.character_world: A connect-the-dots fox who loves spotting how things 'go together the same way'.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — analogies are data {A,B,C, answer, distractors, relationType}; pure tap; images from vocab.
designs.distinctiveness: Relational mapping / analogical reasoning — the child must extract the RELATION from the first pair and transfer it, not match a feature. Distinct from match-pairs (template) which pairs identical/associated items with no second-order relation transfer. Closest neighbor is logic-deduction-09 (sequence rule), separated by: analogy is a 1:1 relation across two pairs, sequence is iterating a transformation.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 2x2 grid of picture slots, one empty, choice row. CA5: fox character, paired-item art sets (animal/baby, tool/use, animal/home), glowing relation-link line, zap effect on correct.

designs.name: Crack the Pattern Code
designs.mechanic: A short sequence follows a hidden transformation rule (shapes growing by one side, numbers +2, colors rotating, rotation by 90°). The child must INFER the rule and tap which item comes NEXT from choices — and for older grades, also tap a 'missing middle' term. The rule is never stated.
designs.fun_no_competition: The detective satisfaction of cracking a growing pattern; the sequence 'completes itself' with a marching animation when right, and the secret rule reveals as a little tag ('+2 each time!').
designs.character_world: A code-breaking raccoon spy decoding 'secret pattern messages'.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — sequences generated from a parameterized rule; choices include near-miss distractors; tap-only.
designs.distinctiveness: Sequence rule-induction with a TRANSFORMATION (not just AB-AB repeat). Distinct from existing pattern-train apps (those mostly repeat a fixed unit) because the rule is a growing/changing transformation the child must deduce. Separated from analogy (logic-08): analogy maps one relation across a pair; this iterates a rule along a sequence and may probe an interior term.
designs.asset_idea: stub: row of shape/number tiles + '?' + choices. CA5: raccoon spy with decoder goggles, growing-shape and numeral tile sets, secret-message scroll backdrop, rule-reveal tag.

designs.name: Whodunit Story Clues
designs.mechanic: A short illustrated mini-mystery ('Who ate the cookies?') gives 2-3 picture/text clues drawn from the story ('the thief left muddy paw prints', 'it was tall enough to reach the shelf'). The child cross-references clues against 3-4 suspect characters and taps the only one who fits ALL clues. Tapping a suspect highlights which clue rules them out.
designs.fun_no_competition: Solving the gentle mystery and watching the culprit sheepishly confess ('it was me!'); each clue you use to rule out a suspect crosses them off with a fun stamp — true detective delight, no timer.
designs.interaction: tap a suspect; clues highlight; tap to accuse the one fitting all clues
designs.character_world: A kid-detective duo (a curious cat and a magnifying-glass mouse) solving cozy neighborhood mysteries.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — suspects carry attribute tags, clues are predicates; elimination logic + TTS for clue read-aloud; needs illustrated suspects/scenes.
designs.distinctiveness: Narrative inference + elimination drawn from text/illustration evidence — instantiates RL inference (using key details to answer who/what/why). Distinct from logic-deduction-01 (abstract item-assignment grid) because clues come from a STORY and require reading-comprehension inference, not just attribute matching. Distinct from spot-the-impossible (10) which is anomaly, not multi-clue elimination.
designs.asset_idea: stub: clue list + suspect row + accuse buttons. CA5: cat+mouse detectives, 4 suspect characters with distinguishing traits (tall/short, muddy paws, etc.), cookie-jar scene, cross-off stamp + confession animation.

designs.name: Make the Statement True (Fix the Equation)
designs.mechanic: A math equation is shown FALSE on purpose ('4 + 3 = 6') with one element draggable/swappable — the child reasons what to change to make it true (swap the 6 for a 7, or add/remove a counter from a group). The equation only 'locks' (glows green, characters cheer) when the relationship is genuinely true. Includes choosing the right comparison symbol (<, =, >) to make a statement true.
designs.fun_no_competition: The deeply satisfying moment the wobbling 'wrong' equation snaps level and glows true; the equal sign does a little balancing animation — fixing it yourself feels like solving a riddle.
designs.interaction: drag to swap a numeral/counter, or tap to choose <, =, >
designs.character_world: A wobbly tightrope-walking sign character who 'can't balance until the math is true'.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — truth check is arithmetic; draggable numerals/symbols are DOM; instant re-evaluation on change.
designs.distinctiveness: Repair-to-truth — the child must reason backward from a desired truth-state to the needed change, the inverse of computing a sum. Distinct from logic-deduction-04 (judge true/false) because here the child must ACT to FIX it. No template does equation/relation repair. Instantiates the meaning of the equal sign and comparison reasoning.
designs.asset_idea: stub: equation with one swappable slot + numeral/symbol palette. CA5: tightrope equal-sign character, counter groups, swappable numeral tiles, <,=,> symbol tokens, balance-snap + cheer animation.

designs.name: Even/Odd Pair-Up Reasoning
designs.mechanic: A pile of objects is shown; the child must decide if the amount is EVEN or ODD — by pairing them up (tap to draw a 'buddy line' between two) and reasoning whether anyone is left alone. If one is left without a partner it's odd; all paired means even. Then they tap EVEN or ODD and the leftover (or lack of) is the proof.
designs.fun_no_competition: The little objects buddy-up with happy faces; the lonely leftover one looks sad-but-cute until the child correctly calls 'ODD!' and it gets a high-five — the proof is visible and adorable.
designs.interaction: tap two objects to pair them (draws a buddy line), then tap EVEN / ODD
designs.character_world: A friendship-themed world where objects 'just want a buddy' and the child helps figure out if everyone has one.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — pairing tracked client-side; parity computed from count; SVG buddy-lines; simple state.
designs.distinctiveness: Deductive even/odd via the pairing argument — instantiates 2.OA.C.3 specifically through the 'is anyone left over?' reasoning, not memorized rules. Distinct from any counting template because the child constructs the PROOF (the pairing) and reasons from a leftover. No template pairs-to-deduce a parity property.
designs.asset_idea: stub: scattered dots + EVEN/ODD buttons. CA5: cute object characters (socks/mittens that naturally pair), buddy-line connector with little heart, lonely-leftover sad-then-happy face, high-five effect.

designs.name: Build It Like Mine
designs.mechanic: A character shows a finished tower made of N stacked blocks (or a scattered set of N items). The child drags blocks onto their own empty plate, one at a time, until their stack has EXACTLY the same number as the model. No counting prompt — the child reproduces the quantity to make a twin.
designs.fun_no_competition: The 'it's a twin!' moment when both stacks line up identical, the character grins and the two towers do a little matching wobble.
designs.character_world: Twin Bears each building a matching block tower so they look the same
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — DOM blocks, drag-to-slot, compare count of placed vs model
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is build-a-buddy/build-a-world, but those are open creative assembly with no correctness target. Here the model defines a precise quantity the child must REPRODUCE (one-to-one to a shown set) — equality of count is the whole win, not free building. Separation: a model exists and yours must equal it.
designs.asset_idea: stub: colored rectangle blocks + two bear sprites. CA5 art: a friendly bear holding a finished block tower, an empty matching plate, sparkle-twin effect

designs.name: Copy the Bead String
designs.mechanic: A model necklace shows a color/shape bead pattern (red-blue-red-blue-yellow). The child threads beads onto their own empty string by tapping a bead palette, reproducing the same sequence in the same order. Correctness = exact ordered match, not just same beads.
designs.fun_no_competition: The necklace clasps shut with a sparkle when the order matches the model exactly, and the character proudly wears the twin necklace.
designs.character_world: A friendly fox who wants a necklace that matches its best friend's
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — ordered array compare, bead palette taps append to string
designs.distinctiveness: Distinct from sort-home (no categorizing into bins) and from match-pairs (no pairing). Closest is build-a-buddy decoration, but here ORDER and SEQUENCE must replicate a model exactly. Separation: it's reproduction of an ordered pattern (AB/ABC/AABB structure).
designs.asset_idea: stub: colored circle beads on a line. CA5 art: fox holding model necklace, empty string, palette of bead colors/shapes

designs.name: Echo the Word
designs.mechanic: A character shows a short CVC/sight word made of letter tiles in a display strip. The child drags letter tiles from a scrambled tray into their own empty strip to reproduce the EXACT same word, letter-for-letter, in order. Copying spelling, not decoding from a picture.
designs.fun_no_competition: The copied word glows and the character reads it aloud, the two identical words high-five — 'you wrote my word!'.
designs.character_world: A parrot who shows a word and wants the child to 'echo' it letter for letter
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — ordered letter-tile compare, TTS on success
designs.distinctiveness: Distinct from existing word-builders that prompt by picture/sound. Here the model word is SHOWN and you copy it tile-by-tile — pure letter-sequence replication (handwriting-copy analog, digital). Separation: reproduce a visible written model exactly.
designs.asset_idea: stub: model word strip + scrambled tile tray. CA5 art: parrot holding a word card, empty strip, echo-glow effect

designs.name: Mirror Move Dance
designs.mechanic: A character strikes a pose / makes a sequence of arm positions on a body-grid (left arm up, right arm out). The child taps the mirror-figure to reproduce the MIRRORED pose (as if facing the character in a mirror) — left/right swapped. Reproduce the model with left-right reflection. Make the L-R reflection produce a correctness check on geometric position (the reflected pose maps to a mirrored cell), so it instantiates 1.G.A.2 reasoning rather than just imitating a pose; otherwise narrow.
designs.fun_no_competition: When the mirror pose matches, the two dancers freeze in a perfect mirrored pose and confetti drops — the twinning delight of 'we're mirror partners!'.
designs.character_world: A dance partner facing the child across a mirror, doing copy-me poses
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — discrete pose slots, compare with L-R swapped target
designs.distinctiveness: A reflection/mimic of a body configuration with the L-R swap that defines a true mirror. Not in any template. Closest is mirror-butterfly (axis reflection) but this is a discrete pose-copy with the mirror-rule taught explicitly through facing dance partners. Separation: reproduce a configuration under reflection across the child's body axis.
designs.asset_idea: stub: two facing stick-figures with selectable arm/leg positions. CA5 art: cute dancer + mirror-partner, pose-snap freeze

designs.name: Copy the Skyline (Bar Match)
designs.mechanic: A model shows a row of buildings/towers of given heights (3 tall, 1 short, 2 medium). The child drags or taps to set each of their OWN towers to the SAME height as the matching model tower — reproducing a set of measured heights side by side.
designs.fun_no_competition: When every tower matches its model height, the two skylines light their windows in sync at dusk — twin-city delight.
designs.character_world: A city-builder mouse making a mirror-city across the river that must look the same
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — per-bar height set, compare each to model height
designs.distinctiveness: Replicate a multi-bar height profile — distinct from chart-count (no data-counting; you copy heights) and from build-a-world (heights must precisely match a model). Separation: faithful reproduction of relative lengths/heights (measurement & comparison via copying).
designs.asset_idea: stub: rows of resizable bar-buildings. CA5 art: mouse architect, two skylines across a river, windows-light-up effect

designs.name: Replicate the Pattern Block Picture
designs.mechanic: A model picture is built from pattern-block shapes (a fish made of 1 triangle + 2 squares + a hexagon) shown on a board. The child drags the same shapes onto their empty board in the same positions/orientations to reproduce the picture — composing shapes to match a model.
designs.fun_no_competition: Final shape snaps in and the picture comes alive (the fish swims) — the joy of rebuilding the character's shape-picture exactly.
designs.character_world: A shape-artist octopus who makes pattern-block pictures for the child to copy
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — drag shape sprites to grid slots, check shape-in-slot match
designs.distinctiveness: Compose-shapes-to-replicate; distinct from build-a-buddy (free composition) because positions/shapes must match a precise model, and distinct from sort-home. Separation: 2D shape composition that reproduces a given figure (composing/decomposing shapes).

designs.name: Copy the Caterpillar (Array Twin)
designs.mechanic: A model shows an arrangement laid out in rows and columns (3 rows of 4 dots). The child taps an empty grid to reproduce the EXACT same rows-and-columns array — same number of rows, same per-row count — making a twin array.
designs.fun_no_competition: The two caterpillars (each made of the array dots) wriggle in sync once they match — the joy of perfectly matched twin grids.
designs.character_world: Two caterpillar friends whose body-segments must match in rows and columns
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — grid tap, compare row/col occupancy to model
designs.distinctiveness: Reuses array structure but as REPLICATE-THE-STRUCTURE, not build-to-a-number or repeated-addition. Closest is the existing E13 build-the-array, which fills to R×C from a prompt; here you copy a SHOWN array's exact shape. Separation: structural replication of a 2D arrangement.

designs.name: Serve the Customer
designs.mechanic: A customer steps to your shop counter and asks for something using a rule ("I'd like THREE red apples, please" or "Can I have the thing that starts with /b/?"). The child applies the rule to assemble the order on a tray and hands it over.
designs.fun_no_competition: Being the trusted shopkeeper; the customer's warm 'That's exactly right, thank you!' and a happy wave goodbye.
designs.character_world: A cozy corner shop (bakery / fruit stall / pet shop) where friendly animal customers come with requests.

Closest neighbor is the magic-machine template (input→transform→output) and narrate-roleplay-11 (robot instructions), but here the child is the SERVER interpreting a customer's natural-language ask and must satisfy a varying constraint (count, attribute, phoneme), not run a fixed machine or give commands. The conversational request framing is the mechanic.
designs.asset_idea: stub: counter rectangle + 3 placeholder animal customers + item icons. CA5 art: shop scene background, rotating cast of cute animal customers, themed goods (fruit, buns, pet toys).

designs.name: Tell the Robot What to Do
designs.mechanic: A literal-minded robot waits for the child to give it a one-step spoken/chosen command using a target structure (e.g., a prepositional phrase: "Put the ball UNDER the table"). The robot acts it out exactly — comically wrong if the child picks the wrong word.
designs.fun_no_competition: Bossing the silly robot around and watching it hilariously over-obey; the joy of authorship and cause-effect.
designs.character_world: A goofy helper robot that does EXACTLY what you say, no more no less.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — assemble a sentence from word chips, then a short CSS-transition animation moves an object to the chosen relation; TTS reads the command.
designs.distinctiveness: Core is CHILD-AUTHORS-AN-INSTRUCTION (child speaks, character obeys), the reverse of comprehension games where the child obeys. Closest neighbor is narrate-roleplay-02 (serve customer) where the CHILD interprets someone else's request; here the child GIVES the command and watches it enacted. Distinct from all 15 templates — no template has the child issuing imperative language a character performs.
designs.asset_idea: stub: blocky robot + a ball + a table outline. CA5 art: charming boxy robot with movable arm, props (ball, box, hat), simple room set.

designs.name: Answer the Story Character
designs.mechanic: After a short illustrated story is read aloud, a character from the story leans in and ASKS the child a comprehension question about what happened ("Why was I sad at the start?"). The child taps the best answer chip; the character reacts as if the child remembered THEIR story.
designs.fun_no_competition: The character treats you like a friend who paid attention; warm 'You DO remember!' reactions and a little story-callback.
designs.character_world: Short picture-story vignettes (a lost mitten, a shy bug) whose characters turn to ask you about themselves.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — DOM story panels, TTS narration, character-asks dialogue bubble, answer chips.
designs.distinctiveness: Core is COMPREHENSION-AS-CONVERSATION where the in-story character (not a quiz screen) interviews the child. Closest neighbor is the story-maker template, but story-maker has the child BUILD/SEQUENCE a story to watch; here the child RECALLS and answers about a given story through dialogue with its character. No competition/quiz framing — it's a chat.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 3 story panels + a character bust. CA5 art: small illustrated story sets, each with one expressive recurring character who breaks the fourth wall.

designs.name: Make the Puppet Speak
designs.mechanic: The child operates a puppet in a tiny two-character scene: choose what the puppet SAYS next from line options, but only the lines that are polite/appropriate or grammatically right move the conversation forward ("May I please join?" vs "Gimme that!"). The other puppet responds in kind. Tie the polite/appropriate line to an explicit SL.K.6/L.1.1.j convention judgment with a clear correct line, so it instantiates the speaking/language standard rather than open improv.
designs.fun_no_competition: You're the puppeteer voicing a character; the satisfaction of a conversation that flows warmly when you pick kind, clear lines.
designs.character_world: A two-puppet stage (a hand puppet you control + a friend puppet) acting out playground/friendship moments.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — dialogue chips, speech bubbles, TTS for both voices, puppet pose swaps on a stage backdrop.
designs.distinctiveness: Core is CHOOSE-YOUR-CHARACTER'S-LINE in a live two-way exchange where social/grammar appropriateness drives the partner's reaction. Closest neighbor is narrate-roleplay-04 (answer the character), but that's recall Q&A about a past story; here the child PUPPETEERS one speaker in an unfolding present-tense conversation, authoring dialogue. Distinct from all 15 templates — it's improv puppetry.
designs.asset_idea: stub: two puppet heads + stage. CA5 art: a felt puppet stage with two distinct puppets, mouth and emotion variants.

designs.name: Whose Voice? (Read the Feeling)
designs.mechanic: A line of dialogue appears and the child must make the puppet SAY it with the right feeling — choose the emotion (happy/sad/scared/excited) that fits the words and context, then the puppet performs the line in that mood (matching TTS tone + face). Mismatches are gently funny.
designs.fun_no_competition: Being the director of the puppet's performance; the comedy of a 'scared' line said super-happy, and the satisfying right-mood delivery.
designs.character_world: A drama-club puppet rehearsing lines who needs you to coach the feeling.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — emotion chips, puppet face swaps per emotion, TTS pitch/rate adjusted to suggest mood; flag: TTS emotional range is limited, so face + pacing carry most of the expression.
designs.distinctiveness: Core is INTERPRET-TONE-AND-PERFORM: the child reads dialogue for emotional/contextual meaning and DIRECTS the delivery (a performance/expression choice), not a content answer. Closest neighbor is narrate-roleplay-06 (choose the line) which selects WHAT is said; this selects HOW it is said. No template touches prosody/expression. Strong for SL.K.6/fluency-with-expression.
designs.asset_idea: stub: puppet with 4 emotion faces + a tiny stage. CA5 art: theatrical puppet with a full emotion face set, curtain/stage backdrop.

designs.name: Order at the Diner
designs.mechanic: The child is the waiter taking a multi-part spoken order ("I'll have two pancakes AND a milk, please") and must read it back / assemble it correctly, handling conjunctions and quantities. The customer confirms with a happy 'Yes, that's my order!'
designs.fun_no_competition: Being the trusted waiter who gets the whole order right; the customer's beaming 'Perfect, thank you!' and a tip of the hat.
designs.character_world: A bustling-but-friendly little diner with cheerful animal regulars.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — TTS speaks the compound order (with a replay button), food chips dragged onto a tray, count + item validation, customer confirm pose.
designs.distinctiveness: Core is HOLD-AND-REPRODUCE A MULTI-ITEM REQUEST involving conjunctions ('and') and counts — listening-memory + connective comprehension in a service role. Closest neighbor is narrate-roleplay-02 (serve the customer), which applies ONE rule/attribute per request; this requires PARSING A COMPOUND request (multiple items + 'and' + quantities) and reproducing the whole list, exercising connectives and listening span. Distinct enough to stand alone (compound vs single-constraint).
designs.asset_idea: stub: diner counter + food icons + customer. CA5 art: diner set, menu items, rotating animal diners with happy poses.

designs.name: Guide the Lost Traveler
designs.mechanic: A lost character on a simple map asks the child for directions to a destination, and the child gives a step-by-step route by choosing/sequencing direction words ("go LEFT, then UP to the bridge"). The traveler walks exactly the path the child describes.
designs.fun_no_competition: Being the helpful guide who gets a lost friend home; watching the traveler follow YOUR directions and cheer at the destination.
designs.character_world: A friendly lost traveler (a turtle, a little knight) on a storybook map needing your directions.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — grid/path map, direction-word chips sequenced into a route, CSS-stepped character movement, TTS reads the route back.
designs.distinctiveness: Core is PRODUCE-A-SEQUENCE-OF-DIRECTIONS in a help-a-character dialogue; the child authors multi-step spatial instructions and the character executes them. Closest neighbor is narrate-roleplay-03 (tell the robot), but that's a SINGLE one-step preposition command; this is an ORDERED MULTI-STEP route (sequencing + positional/directional language). Distinct from path-journey template — there the player moves along a given path; here the child GENERATES the directions for a character.
designs.asset_idea: stub: simple grid map + a token traveler + landmark icons. CA5 art: charming storybook map (forest paths, bridges) with a sweet recurring traveler character.

designs.name: Retell It to the Next Friend
designs.mechanic: After hearing a short 3-part story, a character who 'missed it' asks the child to retell what happened. The child reconstructs the retelling by choosing the beginning/middle/end statements in order and 'tells' it back; the character reacts to each part as if hearing it fresh.
designs.fun_no_competition: Being the storyteller for a friend who missed out; their gasps and 'then what happened?!' as you tell it, and a happy thanks at the end.
designs.character_world: A friend who napped through the story and now hangs on your every word as you retell it.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — story panels played first, then beginning/middle/end statement chips dragged into order, TTS reads each as the child 'tells' it, listener reactions.
designs.distinctiveness: Core is RETELL-A-STORY-TO-AN-AUDIENCE: the child reproduces a narrative sequence as an act of telling it to a listening character (audience-directed retell with first/next/last structure). Closest neighbor is the story-maker template (build a story to watch) — but story-maker invents/sequences NEW panels; here the child RETELLS a GIVEN story in correct order to a character who responds, which is comprehension + recount, not authoring. Also distinct from narrate-roleplay-04 (single recall question) — this is full sequenced retell.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 3 story panels + a wide-eyed listener bust. CA5 art: short illustrated stories + an expressive listener character (gasp, smile, clap poses).

designs.name: Coach the Robot Chef
designs.mechanic: A robot chef can only follow EXACT recipe commands; the child gives it the right verb each step ("STIR the soup," "POUR the milk," "CHOP the carrot") chosen to match what the picture shows needs doing. Wrong verb = a funny kitchen mishap; right verb = the recipe progresses.
designs.fun_no_competition: Being the head chef coaching a literal robot; the slapstick of a wrong verb (it stirs the dry flour everywhere) and the pride of a finished dish.
designs.character_world: A clanky robot chef in a cozy kitchen who needs your verb-by-verb coaching to cook.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — step picture, action-verb chips, short CSS animation per verb (correct progresses, wrong = comic reset), TTS narrates the command and result.
designs.distinctiveness: Core is CHOOSE-THE-ACTION-VERB-IN-CONTEXT to direct a character's task, building a procedure verb by verb. Closest neighbor is narrate-roleplay-03 (tell the robot — prepositions) and -12 (directions), but this targets ACTION VERBS matched to a depicted need (verb meaning/category in a procedural how-to context), not spatial relations or routes. Distinct from magic-machine (fixed transform) — the child selects the appropriate verb each turn from context, exercising verb vocabulary.
designs.asset_idea: stub: robot chef + pot + ingredient icons. CA5 art: kitchen set, expressive robot chef with action poses, ingredients and recipe stages.

designs.name: Robot Recess
designs.mechanic: The child snaps a sequence of direction tiles (up / down / left / right) into a program strip, then taps GO and watches a robot crawl those exact moves across a grid toward a friend. The move-sequence the child assembles IS the answer; nothing else moves the robot.
designs.fun_no_competition: The wobbly robot reunites with its lost puppy at the goal — a little reunion hug animation when the path is right; a wrong program just bonks gently into a hedge and the child re-orders the tiles. No clock, no fails.
designs.character_world: Bolt the recess robot lost his puppy somewhere on the playground grid.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — CSS grid board, draggable direction-tile strip, step-through CSS transform animation per queued move.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is path-journey, but path-journey advances ONE stop on a FIXED ordered track by answering a question — the child never chooses direction. Here the child authors an OPEN move-program in 2D and the spatial choice (which turns, how many) is the whole task. Separation: programming a route vs. answering-to-advance.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: colored squares + arrow glyphs + a circle robot. CA5: playground-grid backdrop, Bolt sprite walk-cycle, puppy, hedge-bonk pose, reunion hug frame.

designs.name: Park the Truck
designs.mechanic: A parking lot grid; a sign says 'Park BETWEEN the red car and the tree' or 'Park to the LEFT of the bus'. The child drags the truck into the spot that satisfies the spatial relation among existing objects. The relation among landmarks defines the target spot.
designs.fun_no_competition: Park correctly and the truck honks a cheerful toot, headlights blink, the driver waves. Wrong spot just rolls back out with a polite reverse-beep. The satisfaction is tidy fitting-in-place.
designs.character_world: A bustling toy-town parking lot run by a beaver attendant.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — grid lot, draggable truck, validate spot against relational rule.
designs.distinctiveness: Where's-My-Hat (02) places ONE object relative to ONE landmark; this requires resolving a relation among TWO+ landmarks (between, left-of-X-but-right-of-Y), a harder relational-position skill. Sort-home places by category. Separation: multi-landmark relational positioning vs. single-relation placement / category sorting.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: lot grid + colored car blocks + a truck rectangle. CA5: parking-lot scene, trucks/cars, beaver attendant, headlight-blink frames.

designs.name: Treasure Coordinates
designs.mechanic: A pirate map is a labeled grid (columns A-E, rows 1-5). A riddle gives a coordinate ('Dig at B-3') and the child taps that exact cell to reveal what's buried. The child reads the column+row pair to locate the square.
designs.fun_no_competition: Every dig reveals SOMETHING fun — a crab, a boot, a gem — so wrong taps are still little surprises, and the right coordinate unearths the treasure chest with a sparkle. Curiosity, not accuracy-pressure.
designs.character_world: Captain Quill's treasure island, each map a new island.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — labeled CSS grid, tap-to-reveal cell with flip animation.
designs.distinctiveness: Reveal-grid scratches cells to find a hidden picture with no addressing; here the cell is chosen by READING a coordinate pair (column letter × row number), the foundational ordered-pair skill. Separation: coordinate-addressed location vs. blind scratch-reveal.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: lettered/numbered grid + emoji buried items. CA5: parchment map, sand-dig reveal, treasure chest, parrot guide.

designs.name: River Steer
designs.mechanic: A boat floats down a branching number-river; at each fork two channels are labeled with numbers and a prompt asks 'steer toward the BIGGER number' (or the answer to a sum). The child taps the left or right channel to steer, and the boat drifts that way.
designs.fun_no_competition: The river meanders past otters and lily pads; steering correctly opens a scenic channel, a wrong turn just bumps a friendly beaver dam that nudges you back to the fork. The journey downstream is the reward.
designs.character_world: A duckling captain rafting home down Comparison Creek.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — fork = two tappable channel zones, CSS path-follow animation for the boat.
designs.distinctiveness: Path-journey is a single fixed track; this is a BRANCHING route where the child's left/right steering choice determines which way the boat goes — directionality + a math decision fused. Magic-machine transforms an input; here the child chooses a DIRECTION at a junction. Separation: branching directional steering vs. fixed-track advance.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: blue Y-shapes + number labels + a boat dot. CA5: river backdrop tiles, duckling raft, otters/beaver dam, channel-glint.

designs.name: Mail Route
designs.mechanic: A neighborhood map shows houses; a route card lists stops in order ('First Maple St, then Oak St, last the Park'). The child taps the houses in that exact left-to-right/ordinal sequence to plan the delivery route, drawing the path between them.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each delivered letter pops a happy resident at the door (a waving grandma, a kid with a kite). Complete the route and the mail truck does a little victory loop. No timer — re-tap to reorder anytime.
designs.character_world: Pip the postal mouse on her morning round.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — tappable house hotspots, SVG polyline drawn between taps in order.
designs.distinctiveness: Story-maker sequences narrative beats with no map; this sequences SPATIAL STOPS on a layout, so ordinal/sequence words become a physical route. Closest neighbor is path-journey, but here the child CHOOSES which stops and the ORDER over an open map rather than advancing along a pre-drawn line. Separation: ordinal route-planning over a map vs. linear track-advance.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: dots for houses + numbered route line. CA5: town map, mail-mouse truck, waving residents, letter-drop animation.

designs.name: Word Ladder Climb
designs.mechanic: A vertical ladder of rungs; the child climbs UP by tapping rungs in order, and each rung is unlocked by reading a CVC word and tapping it. The spatial climb is upward/downward and the word reading gates the ascent — directionality (up/top, down/bottom) plus decoding. Bind advancement to decoding the rung word (RF.K.3.b) AND naming the above/below position (L.K.1.e), so the vertical axis instantiates a standard rather than decorating climbing.
designs.fun_no_competition: A koala climbs toward a treetop nest of eucalyptus snacks; reaching the TOP rung triggers a happy munch. Climbing back down to look at lower rungs is fine — the tree is to explore.
designs.character_world: Kip the koala climbing the storybook gum tree.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — vertical flex ladder, koala translateY per rung, word-tap unlock.
designs.distinctiveness: This emphasizes the VERTICAL up/down axis (top/bottom/above/below positional language) with a climbing-character, distinct from the horizontal number line (08) and 2D grids. The reading gate is incidental; the spatial axis is the point. Separation: vertical up/down axis travel vs. horizontal/2D navigation.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: stacked rungs + word labels + a koala dot. CA5: gum-tree backdrop, koala climb frames, treetop nest, leaf-munch.

designs.name: Track-Switch Train Dispatcher
designs.mechanic: Trains roll in one at a time on the main line, each carrying a numbered platform sign. You operate the junction by flipping track-switch levers to route the train onto the correct numbered platform siding. Set the switches right and the train chugs home; then the next train approaches.
designs.fun_no_competition: Levers clunk with a chunky toggle sound, the train toots and rolls happily into its bay; trains idle patiently while you decide.
designs.character_world: A miniature railway control tower with big colorful switch levers and cheerful steam engines bearing platform numbers.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — toggle-state levers + CSS path animation along predefined siding rails; route is determined by switch states.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is path-journey, but path-journey moves a single traveler along a route the child draws; here the child does NOT move along a path — they configure SWITCHES at a junction to route a stream of incoming trains by reading their numbers. Separation from sort-home: sort-home drops items into bins; here you set rule-levers and the system carries the item itself.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: rectangles for tracks + toggle squares. CA5 art: railway junction, numbered platforms, friendly engines, signal-box levers.

designs.name: Stamp-Machine Rule Operator
designs.mechanic: Parcels travel down the mailroom belt, each marked with a starting number. You operate a stamp machine set to a posted rule ('+10') and tap each parcel to apply the rule, stamping it with the result before it ships. The same rule applies to a whole batch, so you operate the machine across a sequence of incoming parcels.
designs.fun_no_competition: The stamp comes down with a satisfying THUNK and an ink-puff; the parcel slides off and the next one rolls up at a calm pace.
designs.character_world: A busy-but-gentle post office mailroom with a chunky rubber stamp, a rule placard, and parcels with smiley address labels.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — tap parcel, compute result, animate stamp + reveal stamped numeral; rule is a config value.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is magic-machine, but magic-machine is a single delightful transform per use; here the operator applies a STATED rule repeatedly across a stream of parcels (the running mailroom), and the standard is mental +10/-10. Separation from pop-the-right-ones: you don't pick which to act on — you apply a fixed rule to every item in turn.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: brown box + number label + stamp icon. CA5 art: mailroom belt, ink stamper, parcel sprites, rule placard, outgoing chute.

designs.name: Traffic-Signal Crossing Operator
designs.mechanic: Cars and pedestrians arrive at an intersection holding a small math fact card ('6+4'). You operate the signal by reading the card and tapping the matching numbered light/lane that equals the answer, giving that lane the green to flow through. Keep the crossing running smoothly as demands arrive on each road.
designs.fun_no_competition: Green light glows, the little cars beep happily and roll across; vehicles idle calmly with no honking-rush.
designs.character_world: A friendly town intersection with a crossing-guard's signal box, smiling cars, and pedestrians on each road.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — tap a lane/light, validate against computed answer, CSS car-drive animation across the intersection.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is the train dispatcher (operate-system-03), but the dispatcher routes by reading a single given number; here the operator must COMPUTE a sum/difference to decide which lane to clear, and the system is a four-way intersection with multiple incoming roads. Separation from pop-the-right-ones: you're granting passage to a flow, controlling an ongoing crossing, not popping isolated targets.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: cross-roads diagram + light circles + fact cards. CA5 art: town intersection, traffic-signal box, car/animal sprites, crosswalk.

designs.name: Parcel-Scale Weigh Station
designs.mechanic: Packages roll up to the shipping scale, each needing to be balanced. You operate the weigh station by reading the target weight and tapping unit-weights onto the balance pan until the needle/number matches, then stamping the package 'SHIPPED'. Keep the station running as packages line up.
designs.fun_no_competition: When the scale balances, the needle settles with a gentle 'ding' and the SHIPPED stamp thumps down; packages wait their turn calmly.
designs.character_world: A tidy shipping depot with a big dial scale, unit-weight blocks, package sprites, and a courier who salutes each shipment.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — tap unit-weights onto pan, sum vs target, animate needle/numeral; stamp is overlay.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is the cash-register cashier (operate-system-06), but that composes a money value from coins; here the operator reads and matches a MEASUREMENT (weight on a scale) by adding standard units — distinct measurement strand and a balance-instrument feel. Separation from grow-tend: nothing grows; you balance an instrument repeatedly.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: balance bar + weight blocks + target number. CA5 art: dial weigh-scale, weight blocks, parcels, SHIPPED stamp, courier.

designs.name: Marquee Letter-Tile Sign Operator
designs.mechanic: The theater marquee needs the next show's title posted. A request card shows a word with one or more missing letters (often the beginning/medial/ending sound blank). You operate the sign by reading the word and the picture clue, then sliding the correct letter tiles into the empty marquee slots to spell it. Post the word right and the marquee lights up for the next showing.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each completed title makes the marquee bulbs flicker on with a twinkle and a tiny crowd cheers; sign requests wait patiently on the easel.
designs.character_world: A vintage cinema marquee with rows of letter-slots, a tile rack, and a bow-tied usher who applauds each finished sign.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — drag letter tiles to slots, validate spelling, light-up CSS animation; picture clue is a sprite.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is magic-trace, but magic-trace forms a letter by tracing a stroke; here the operator SELECTS and places letter tiles to complete a word's spelling (CVC sounds) on a marquee that posts a queue of titles — a phonics-spelling station, not a tracing motor task. Separation from story-maker: you're filling exact spelling slots, not composing free sentences.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: empty letter-slots + tile rack. CA5 art: marquee frame with bulbs, letter tiles, picture-clue cards, usher character.

designs.name: Hop Cannon
designs.mechanic: A friendly cannon sits at 0 on a big number line. The child drags a 'power dial' to set how far each hop jumps (1, 2, 5, or 10) and a counter to set how many hops, then fires — the cannonball arcs forward in equal bounces, landing on a glowing target number. Setting hop-size × hop-count so the ball lands exactly on the target IS the answer.
designs.fun_no_competition: The satisfying THWUMP of the launch and the bouncy equal hops that land plumb on the target with a confetti puff. A short shot lands wide and the cannonball just rolls back so the child re-dials — no miss penalty, no clock.
designs.character_world: Pip the squirrel fires acorns from a spring-cannon to reach the marked branch on the number-line tree.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — CSS-positioned number line, two drag sliders (hop-size, hop-count), and a sequence of CSS-keyframe arc hops; landing = hopSize*hopCount computed, not simulated.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is path-journey, but path-journey advances ONE stop per answered question along a fixed track. Here the child deliberately SETS a launch quantity (hop-size and count) before any motion, and the equal-interval arc lands wherever that quantity computes to — a single aimed launch encoding a multiplication/skip-count, not question-by-question advancement.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: a box-cannon rectangle + circle ball + tick number line. CA5 art: spring-loaded acorn cannon, arc-trail sparkles, target branch with a glowing nest.

designs.name: Stretch the Caterpillar
designs.mechanic: A spring-loaded caterpillar's tail is pinned at 0 on a ruler; the child drags its head along the ruler to stretch its body to a target length (e.g., 'make him 8 cm long'). A live readout shows the current length while dragging; releasing locks it. The stretch-length the child stops at IS the answer.
designs.fun_no_competition: The bouncy elastic body that ripples as you stretch and the caterpillar's happy 'just right!' wiggle when the length matches. Overstretch springs back gently — no rush, no penalty.
designs.character_world: Clementine the caterpillar wants to grow to exactly the right size to reach her leaf.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — drag handle sets element width along a ruler; live length readout = pixels mapped to cm; compare on release.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is magic-trace (drawing a guided stroke), but tracing follows a predetermined path shape. Here nothing is traced — the child meters a single elastic LENGTH against a ruler and the measured extent is the whole answer. Distinct from Stretch-band fractions below by measuring a whole-unit length on a ruler, not partitioning a fixed band.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: a rectangle 'body' anchored left + draggable head circle + ruler ticks. CA5 art: stretchy striped caterpillar with a smiley face, segment markers as ruler units, leaf at target.

designs.name: Slingshot to the Tens
designs.mechanic: A slingshot at the left holds a numbered pebble (a two-digit number card). Floating targets on the right are labeled in expanded/place-value forms ('40 + 7', '4 tens 7 ones'). The child pulls the slingshot band back and angles it to aim, then releases; the pebble flies in a computed arc to whichever target the aim points at. Aiming at the equivalent representation IS the answer.
designs.fun_no_competition: The stretchy THWANG of the release and the pebble's gentle arc landing with a satisfying thock on the matching target balloon, which pops into confetti. A miss floats the pebble back to the pouch to re-aim — no clock.
designs.character_world: Bo the bunny launches berries with his slingshot to the matching basket in the sky.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — drag sets pull-distance and angle; on release compute the arc endpoint from angle and pick the nearest target; CSS keyframe arc; no physics engine.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is match-pairs, but match-pairs links two static cards by tapping both. Here the child performs a single deliberate AIM-and-launch — the pull-and-angle set-up directs a projectile to exactly one equivalent target. The physical trajectory, not a tap-pair, carries the matching choice.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: a Y-shaped slingshot rectangle + draggable pouch + floating target circles. CA5 art: leafy slingshot, glossy berry, balloon targets with place-value labels.

designs.name: Stretch-Band Fractions
designs.mechanic: A rubber band is stretched horizontally between 0 and 1 (a whole). The child drags pinch-pegs onto the band to partition it into equal parts, then drags a slider to fill from 0 up to a target point ('shade 3/4'). The fill-stop position on the partitioned band IS the answer.
designs.fun_no_competition: The twangy stretch of the band and the springy click as each peg snaps it into equal segments, then a warm glow filling the shaded part. Wrong fill slides back freely — no clock, no miss-count.
designs.character_world: Twang the cricket plays his fraction-band like a guitar string, dividing it into even frets.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — band is a flex bar; pegs split it into equal CSS segments; a fill overlay slider sets the shaded width; check fill vs. target fraction.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is Pour the Potion (fill a vertical beaker to a fraction), but here the child first PARTITIONS an elastic whole into equal parts by placing pegs, then meters a horizontal fill across those parts — partition-then-fill on a stretched band vs. a pre-marked vertical pour. Distinct from Stretch the Caterpillar by partitioning a fixed 0–1 whole rather than measuring an open length.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: a horizontal band rectangle with 0/1 ends + draggable peg markers + fill overlay. CA5 art: a guitar-string band, frog/cricket strummer, glowing shaded frets.

designs.name: Fill the Ten-Frame Tank
designs.mechanic: A ten-frame is drawn as a clear tank of ten cells; a hose pours glowing dots that fill cells one by one from bottom-left. The child holds to pour and releases to stop, filling the tank to match a target number ('fill to 7'). The number of cells filled when the child stops IS the answer.
designs.fun_no_competition: The bubbly pour and each cell lighting up with a soft pop as it fills, ending on a cheerful 'seven!' callout when it matches. Overfill drains the last cell with a tap — no timer, no fail.
designs.character_world: Dewey the duckling fills his ten-cell pond tray with glowing pondweed bubbles.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — hold-to-pour fills ten-frame cells sequentially; release stops; count filled vs. target; pure DOM cell toggling.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is Funnel the Beads (pour discrete beads to a level line), but that is a single stacking tube. Here the pour fills a structured TEN-FRAME (place-value-of-ten model) cell by cell, so the child meters the pour against the ten-frame's grid — a pour metered against a base-ten structure, tying the physical fill to ten-frame number sense, distinct from a plain tube level.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: a 2x5 cell grid 'tank' + a hose rectangle + dot fill. CA5 art: clear ten-frame aquarium, glowing bubble dots, duckling with a watering hose.

designs.name: Pour to Balance the Scale
designs.mechanic: A two-pan balance has a fixed weight on the left pan; the right pan holds an empty measuring cup with unit lines. The child tilts a jug to pour water into the right cup, watching the beam tilt; they stop pouring when the beam is level. The water level poured to balance (equal to the left weight) IS the answer. Drop 3.MD.A.2; retarget the pour-to-balance to a grade-1 equality reading (the levels are equal = 1.OA.D.7 meaning-of-equal) and require the child to confirm equality, so it instantiates rather than touches.
designs.fun_no_competition: The glug of the pour and the slow swing of the beam toward level, with a gentle 'balanced!' chime and a glow when both sides match. Overpour dips the pan and a tap drains a unit — no rush, no fail.
designs.character_world: Bea the bear balances honey against river-stones on her kitchen scale.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — pour increments a fill height that drives the beam rotation (CSS); level when fill = target; graduated cup gives the readout.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is Stack 'til It Tips (add discrete blocks to balance), but that meters by adding counted whole-value blocks. Here the child meters a CONTINUOUS pour against a beam-balance and reads a measured liquid amount — pour-to-balance vs. stack-to-balance — combining the pour metaphor with equality/measurement on a graduated cup.
designs.asset_idea: Stub: a beam rectangle on a fulcrum, a fixed weight square, a graduated cup rectangle + jug. CA5 art: honey jar, rustic balance scale, river-stone weights, golden glow.

designs.name: Echo the Beat
designs.mechanic: A character taps out a short rhythm pattern on colored pads (e.g. red-red-blue). The pads light and sound in sequence. The child then taps the SAME pads back in the same order to echo it. Pattern length grows by one as the child succeeds; the child sets the pace tapping back. Tie the reproduced sequence to a count/order readout (K.CC.A.1 count to a number, each pad = next number) so the Simon-echo instantiates rote-count/sequence rather than pure memory.
designs.fun_no_competition: It feels like a musical game of follow-the-leader with a friend — each round adds one more note so you get to play a longer and longer little tune, and the pads sing back to you.
designs.character_world: A friendly frog on a lily pad with glowing musical lily-pad buttons
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — WebAudio tones per pad, sequence playback with delays (no timer, child-paced response), DOM pad highlights
designs.distinctiveness: Not match-pairs (no pairing) and not magic-machine (no transform). The core is a call-and-RESPONSE memory-of-order: reproduce an ordered auditory/visual sequence. Closest neighbor is sticker-album sequencing, but that is free placement; here the model is given and must be echoed back in exact order, and the content is sound+order not pictures.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 3 colored squares that flash. CA5: frog conductor, 4 glowing lily-pad pads with press/ripple states, twinkle sparkle on correct echo

designs.name: Which Sound Was That?
designs.mechanic: A sound plays (animal call, instrument, or environmental sound) and three picture choices appear. The child listens, then taps the picture that made the sound. Replayable as often as wanted by tapping the ear button. Pure listen-then-identify, fully child-paced. Narrow to a phonological-awareness target (identify the sound a letter/animal name begins with, RF.K.1.a/RF.K.2 readiness) rather than generic environmental SFX, so it instantiates a phonics standard.
designs.fun_no_competition: It's a guessing game with your ears — the moment a 'moo' resolves into the cow is a happy little 'aha', and you can replay the sound as many times as you like, no rush.
designs.character_world: A big-eared listening fox holding a cupped ear
designs.web_shell_feasibility: needs-richer-runtime — requires a curated library of clean sound-effect clips (animal/instrument); WebAudio can play them but the assets must be sourced/licensed
designs.distinctiveness: Closest is i-spy-scene/pop-the-right-ones, but those are VISUAL search.
