Here the stimulus is AUDITORY and the visual is the answer set — the child decodes a sound, not scans a picture. The discrimination skill is auditory, the input modality reversed from every existing template.
designs.asset_idea: stub: ear button + 3 pictures. CA5: listening fox with ear-cup animation, sound-wave ripple, picture choice cards (needs SFX audio pack)

designs.name: Conduct the Pattern
designs.mechanic: An AB/ABB/ABC rhythm pattern is shown as a row of colored sound-shapes that play in a loop (boom-tick-boom-tick). The next two slots are blank. The child taps from a palette of sound-shapes to FILL the blanks so the rhythm pattern continues correctly; the loop replays with their additions. Swap the thin K.OA.A.1 tag for the pattern-extension reading it actually instantiates (continue a repeating AB/ABC sequence — extend-the-pattern, aligns with operations/algebraic readiness K.OA/2.OA.C.3 patterning).
designs.fun_no_competition: You're conducting a tiny beat-loop and the moment your added sounds keep the groove going feels like dropping the right note into a song; the loop grooves on with your additions.
designs.character_world: A penguin conductor with a baton in front of a sound-shape music staff
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — WebAudio distinct tones per shape, looping playback, DOM pattern row with fillable slots
designs.distinctiveness: The platform has visual pattern-train (silent visual sequence). This makes the pattern AUDITORY+temporal — the child extends a repeating rhythm they hear looping, judging by ear/beat what comes next. The 'continue the pattern' core is real but the medium (a looping rhythm) and the judging sense (auditory) are new.
designs.asset_idea: stub: colored shape row + palette. CA5: penguin conductor with baton swing, glowing sound-shapes (boom/tick/ding), looping pulse highlight

designs.name: Blend it with Taps
designs.mechanic: Three sound buttons each hold one phoneme (/c/ /a/ /t/). The child taps them left-to-right one at a time, hearing each sound; then taps a big 'blend' arrow that sweeps the buttons together faster and faster (child-controlled) until the whole word says itself. Then they tap the matching picture.
designs.fun_no_competition: Tapping the sweep arrow makes the three sounds slide together and 'magically' become a word — the satisfying moment /c/.../a/.../t/ snaps into 'cat' feels like a tiny spell working.
designs.character_world: A gentle sound-wizard owl with three glowing sound-stones
designs.web_shell_feasibility: needs-richer-runtime — isolated-phoneme TTS is unreliable (consonants spoken as letter names per the project's RF.K.2.c finding); requires pre-recorded phoneme audio clips per locale rather than browser TTS
designs.distinctiveness: Not the CVC builder (no letter tiles, no spelling). The core is auditory phoneme blending PACED by the child's taps — sounds in order, then a sweep that fuses them. The skill is hearing separate sounds become a word through a temporal sweep, which no existing template does (build-a-buddy assembles parts; this fuses sounds).
designs.asset_idea: stub: 3 sound dots + arrow. CA5: wizard owl, 3 glowing rune-stones with pulse, sweep-trail effect, picture target cards (needs phoneme audio pack)

designs.name: Stretch the Word
designs.mechanic: A picture-word is shown. The child presses and HOLDS a stretch-button: as they hold, the spoken word slows and pulls apart into its sounds (rubber-band style), and dots appear for each phoneme heard. Releasing snaps it back to the whole word. The child then taps the dot-count that matches.
designs.fun_no_competition: Holding the button stretches 'fish' into f-i-sh like pulling taffy, and the sound-dots pop out one by one — it's playful and physical, and letting go snaps the word back together with a boing.
designs.character_world: A stretchy rubber-band cat that pulls words apart
designs.web_shell_feasibility: needs-richer-runtime — smooth time-stretch of speech needs pre-segmented per-phoneme audio (or a playbackRate trick on recorded clips); browser TTS can't cleanly stretch into phonemes
designs.distinctiveness: A press-and-hold 'stretchy speech' interaction — phoneme segmentation made tangible by slowing the word and counting the sounds that pop out. No template uses hold-to-stretch audio. Distinct from blend (05) which fuses sounds; this SEGMENTS them, and the gesture (hold/stretch) is the core.
designs.asset_idea: stub: hold-button + dot row. CA5: rubber-band cat stretch frames, taffy-pull word visual, phoneme dots popping, snap-back boing effect

designs.name: Add with Drumrolls
designs.mechanic: Two number cards show (3 + 2). The child taps a drum 3 times (first group, low drum), then taps a second drum 2 times (second group, high drum), and the taps accumulate into one counting line; the total is heard counting up across both groups (one-two-three... four-five) and the friend announces the sum.
designs.fun_no_competition: Two little drum-rolls flow into one big count and the total pops out with a cymbal — joining 3 and 2 sounds like one song made of two phrases, and you played both.
designs.character_world: A two-drum panda drummer (one low, one high)
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — WebAudio two drum samples + ascending count tones, TTS for the sum, DOM tap accumulation
designs.distinctiveness: Not magic-machine (no transform box) and not match-pairs. Addition is performed as TWO rhythmic groups of taps that join into one continuous count — the 'putting together' is literally heard as one drum-roll flowing into the next. Counting-on / joining as a temporal sequence is the distinct mechanic.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 2 drums + count row. CA5: panda drummer, two drums (low/high) with hit frames, accumulating count dots, cymbal-crash sparkle

designs.name: Where's the Sound?
designs.mechanic: A target sound (the first sound of a word, given as a clean syllable cue like 'sss') plays. Three picture-words are shown. The child taps each picture to HEAR it spoken, listens for which one BEGINS with that sound, and taps it. The beginning-sound is judged purely by ear.
designs.fun_no_competition: Tapping each picture lets you 'try it out loud', and catching the word that starts the same way feels like an ear-detective solving a little mystery — replay all you want, no clock.
designs.character_world: A magnifying-glass-eared detective hedgehog
designs.web_shell_feasibility: needs-richer-runtime — reliable onset cue ('sss', 'mmm') is fine via TTS for continuants but stops (/b/,/t/) are unreliable; best with curated onset audio for stop consonants
designs.distinctiveness: The platform's beginning-sound activity is visual/letter-anchored. This version is listen-first: the child hears words and isolates onsets by ear with no letters shown — auditory onset detection. Distinct from which-sound (06, environmental sounds) because the stimulus is a SPEECH onset cue and the child probes words by listening.
designs.asset_idea: stub: ear cue + 3 pictures. CA5: detective hedgehog with monocle, sound-wave cue puff, picture cards with tap-glow

designs.name: Hum the Pattern Up & Down
designs.mechanic: A growing/shrinking sound pattern plays where pitch tracks a quantity (low note = small, high note = big). The child hears a sequence (small-big-small) and arranges three picture-objects of different sizes in the order the sounds went, using pitch as the size cue. Bind the pitch-to-size order to a verified size-comparison correctness check (order objects by size = K.MD.A.2), so the cross-modal cue instantiates the measurement standard rather than decorating it.
designs.fun_no_competition: Low notes feel small and high notes feel big — when you line up the objects to match the tune you 'see the sound', and the row plays back its little melody to confirm.
designs.character_world: A whale singing low-to-high bubble-notes
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — WebAudio pitch sweep tones, DOM drag-order of 3 size-graded picture objects, playback confirmation
designs.distinctiveness: Maps an auditory dimension (pitch) onto a math attribute (size/quantity) and asks the child to ORDER objects by decoding the sound sequence. Distinct from big-small/sort templates which are silent-visual; here the ordering information arrives as sound and must be translated. Cross-modal pitch-to-size ordering is novel.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 3 pitch dots + 3 objects. CA5: singing whale, rising/falling bubble-notes, size-graded object cards (small/med/big), order-confirm shimmer

designs.name: Read it to the Beat
designs.mechanic: A short decodable sentence is shown with one tap-pad per word. The child taps each pad in order at their own pace; each tap speaks that word and the character takes one step. Tapping word-by-word in sequence reads the sentence aloud and walks the character to the end — a paced, left-to-right read.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each tap makes the character take a step and says the word, so reading the sentence walks your friend across the page to a little goal — finishing the line feels like completing a short journey you read aloud.
designs.character_world: A snail crossing a leaf, one word-step at a time
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — browser TTS per word, DOM word-pads in order, character step animation; decodable sentences from existing word data
designs.distinctiveness: Different from story-maker (assembling a story) — this is concept-of-print: one tap = one word, in order, left to right, with one-to-one speech-to-word correspondence. The temporal one-tap-per-word pacing instantiates tracking print, which no template targets. The rhythm IS reading word-by-word.
designs.asset_idea: stub: word pads + walker dot. CA5: stepping snail frames, word-pads that light when tapped, finish-leaf with sparkle

designs.name: Tap the Tens & Ones Beat
designs.mechanic: A two-digit number shows (e.g. 23). The child taps a deep 'TEN' gong for each ten (low boom × 2) then a light 'ONE' tick for each one (× 3). The two grouped rhythms — booms then ticks — sonify the place value, and the friend says 'two tens and three ones, twenty-three' when the beat matches.
designs.fun_no_competition: Big booms for tens and tiny ticks for ones make a number into a little rhythm pattern — 23 has its own beat, and tapping it out makes place value feel like drumming.
designs.character_world: A two-gong tortoise: a big gong (tens) and a tiny bell (ones)
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — WebAudio low gong + high tick samples, TTS for the decomposition, DOM tap grouping with place-value check
designs.distinctiveness: Place value performed as a TWO-LAYER rhythm (heavy beats for tens, light beats for ones). Distinct from the platform's visual place-value build-on-columns engine — here the decomposition is heard and tapped, not stacked as blocks. Sonifying tens-vs-ones as distinct beat weights is a new mechanic.
designs.asset_idea: stub: big gong + small bell + count. CA5: tortoise drummer, large gong with deep-ripple, small bell with light-ring, tens/ones beat dots

designs.name: Equal Beats
designs.mechanic: Two short rhythm rows play (e.g. left = 3 claps, right = 5 claps). The child listens to both, then taps the side with MORE beats (or a 'same' button when equal). Each row replays on tap; comparison is made by ear, counting beats, not by seeing a quantity.
designs.fun_no_competition: Listening to two little beat-bursts and feeling which one is longer is like comparing two drum solos — replay them as much as you want and the friend nods when you pick the bigger beat.
designs.character_world: Two friendly drum-bugs side by side, each with its own beat
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — WebAudio clap sequences per side, replay on tap, DOM more/same/less choice
designs.distinctiveness: Compare-quantity exists as silent visual (more-less/big-small). Here the two quantities are presented as RHYTHMIC beat-sequences and compared by listening and counting beats — auditory magnitude comparison. The stimulus modality and the count-by-listening are new versus every visual comparison template.
designs.asset_idea: stub: two drum buttons + choice. CA5: two drum-bugs, beat-burst ripple per side, 'more/same' big buttons, winner-side gentle glow

designs.name: Share It Fair
designs.mechanic: N cookies sit on a tray and M friends wait with empty plates. The child drags cookies one-to-one onto plates, dealing them out until each friend's plate has an equal share. The remainder (if any) stays on the tray as 'leftovers nobody can split,' surfacing partitive division.
designs.fun_no_competition: Every friend smiles and says 'thank you, that's fair!' when all plates match; the leftover cookie gets a giggle ('save it for later').
designs.character_world: A picnic blanket with woodland friends (fox, rabbit, bear) holding empty plates.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — count-based equality check on M drop-zones, no physics.
designs.distinctiveness: Closest neighbor is sort-home (drag item to its bin), but here the bins (plates) must end up with EQUAL counts and the skill is partitive division, not categorization — placement is constrained by an equity rule across all targets simultaneously, not by an attribute of each item. Separation: sort-home checks each item against a fixed category; this checks the whole distribution for equality.
designs.asset_idea: stub: colored circles as cookies + 3 plate rectangles labeled with animal faces. CA5: cookie sprite, 3 seated woodland animals each with a plate, happy/neutral face swap.

designs.name: Everyone Gets the Same
designs.mechanic: Three party bags must each end up identical. A palette holds stickers, candies, and toys; the child fills bag 1, and bags 2 and 3 must be built to MATCH it exactly (same items, same counts). Mismatched bags glow until corrected — a one-to-one correspondence / equal-sets task.
designs.fun_no_competition: When all three bags are twins, the friends hold them up together and confetti-free sparkles say 'we all got the same!'
designs.character_world: A birthday party where three friends each wait for a goodie bag.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — compare item-count maps per bag against the reference bag.
designs.distinctiveness: Unlike match-pairs (link A to its single partner) this requires reproducing a MULTI-ITEM set across multiple recipients so all sets are equal — the unit of fairness is a whole bag, not a pair. Separation from #01: here counts-per-item-type must match a reference set, not just total count be equal.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 3 bag outlines + a tray of distinct emoji-like items. CA5: open party bags, item sprites (star sticker, gummy, toy car), 3 kid characters.

designs.name: What Each Guest Needs
designs.mechanic: Each guest at a table states a need in a speech bubble ('I'm thirsty,' 'I dropped my fork,' 'I can't see'). The child reads/hears the need and delivers the ONE item that solves it (cup, fork, lamp) from a shared tray — applying a need→item rule per character.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each helped guest beams and the need-bubble turns into a heart; helping the whole table fills a warm 'everyone's happy' banner.
designs.character_world: A cozy cafe with animal guests asking for help.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — need-string maps to correct item id; TTS for the bubble.
designs.distinctiveness: Feed-the-friend gives a creature any items it eats; here each delivery must satisfy a SPECIFIC stated need read from text, making it a rule-application + reading-comprehension task, not appetite. Separation from sort-home: the target isn't a category bin, it's a character whose need is described in language.
designs.asset_idea: stub: speech bubbles with text + tray of labeled items. CA5: seated cafe animals, item sprites (cup, fork, lamp, napkin), happy-face swap.

designs.name: The Matchmaker
designs.mechanic: Each character holds half of a relationship ('I have the dog' — who has the bone? 'I'm the key' — who's the lock?). The child connects every character to their relationship partner by a stated semantic rule, draining the unmatched line until all are paired.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each matched pair does a little hug-bounce; 'best friends found!' when the whole crowd is paired.
designs.character_world: A crowd of mixed-up characters looking for their other half.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — relationship adjacency map; tap-A-then-B draws an SVG line, validate the pair.
designs.distinctiveness: Unlike match-pairs (identical/visual pairs like memory) the link is a SEMANTIC RELATIONSHIP (owner→pet, tool→use, part→whole) — a vocabulary-relationship skill among characters, where pairing resolves a social want. Separation from #03: there a need maps to an inanimate item; here a CHARACTER maps to a partner CHARACTER by relationship.
designs.asset_idea: stub: two columns of labeled tokens. CA5: pairable character/object sprites (dog↔bone, key↔lock, glove↔hand).

designs.name: Make It Even
designs.mechanic: Two friends start with UNEQUAL piles (5 vs 3 marbles). The child moves marbles one at a time from the bigger pile to the smaller until both piles are equal — an averaging/equalizing action that surfaces 'how many to move to make them the same.'
designs.fun_no_competition: The two friends end up grinning at twin piles — 'now it's fair!' — and high-five.
designs.character_world: Two friends sharing a bag of marbles/blocks.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — two counters, transfer-on-drag, check equality.
designs.distinctiveness: No template moves quantity BETWEEN recipients to equalize; #01/#02 deal from a shared source, this redistributes existing unequal holdings (the difference, halved). Separation from #01: the source is another friend's pile, and the math is equalizing a difference, not partitive division of a single source.
designs.asset_idea: stub: two pile-zones with counters. CA5: marble/block sprites, two kid characters, balance-scale motif.

designs.name: Give Each a Fraction of the Set
designs.mechanic: A bowl of 12 grapes must be shared so each of 3 friends gets a NAMED fraction of the set ('give Mia one-third'). The child counts out the correct number (12 ÷ 3 = 4) into each friend's cup — fractions OF A SET tied to equal sharing.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each friend's cup fills to the exact fair share and they toast; 'one-third each — perfectly fair!'
designs.character_world: Snack time sharing a bowl of fruit fairly.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — count items into N cups, compare to total/N.
designs.distinctiveness: #05 partitions a single whole; this partitions a SET by a named unit fraction, bridging division and fraction language. Separation from #01: the prompt is fraction-named ('one third of these'), training set-fraction vocabulary, not free equal-deal.
designs.asset_idea: stub: bowl + 3 cups + count readout. CA5: grape/berry sprites, three friends with cups.

designs.name: The Right Gift
designs.mechanic: Each friend has a hint about what they'd love ('she loves things that float,' 'he likes round things'). The child reads the clue and gifts the ONE item from the shop that fits the described attribute/category — inference from a textual clue to a category.
designs.fun_no_competition: The friend gasps with delight and hugs the gift — 'you knew exactly what I'd love!'
designs.character_world: A gift shop where you pick presents for friends by their hints.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — clue maps to an attribute tag; items carry tags; validate match.
designs.distinctiveness: Unlike #03 (need→fixed solution item) the gift is chosen by INFERRING a category from a descriptive clue ('things that float'), a comprehension + attribute-classification task with multiple valid-looking candidates. Separation from sort-home: the bin isn't shown; it's described and must be inferred per character.
designs.asset_idea: stub: clue bubbles + shelf of tagged items. CA5: friend characters, shop shelf, gift items (boat, ball, kite).

designs.name: Take Turns Fairly
designs.mechanic: One toy, several friends. The child arranges a turn-ORDER so each friend gets exactly one turn before anyone repeats, following an ordinal rule ('the youngest goes first,' 'go in a circle'). Building the fair rotation is the skill — ordinal/sequence reasoning about fairness. Tie the rotation to ordinal-number labeling (first/second/third turn = ordinal/count sequence, K.CC.B.4) so building the turn-order instantiates ordinal reasoning rather than touching fairness.
designs.fun_no_competition: Everyone gets their turn and waves 'thanks for sharing!' — the rotation loops with happy faces, nobody left out.
designs.character_world: Friends sharing one swing/scooter and taking fair turns.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — order array, validate one-turn-each + ordinal rule.
designs.distinctiveness: No template builds a fair SEQUENCE/rotation; path-journey moves one actor along a fixed path, whereas this ORDERS multiple actors so each is included once by a rule. Separation from #04 (spatial adjacency): this is temporal order/turn-fairness, not seating adjacency.
designs.asset_idea: stub: numbered turn-slots + friend tokens. CA5: a swing, queue of kid friends, '1st/2nd/3rd' tags.

designs.name: How Are They Feeling?
designs.mechanic: A short illustrated mini-scene shows characters in a social moment (one sharing, one left out). The child reads/hears 2-3 sentences and taps the face/word that names how a named character FEELS and why — character-feeling comprehension driving a kind response.
designs.fun_no_competition: Choosing the kind response makes the left-out friend brighten and join in — the scene warms up, 'now everyone feels included.'
designs.character_world: Little classroom/playground vignettes about feelings and kindness.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — static scene + sentence + tap-the-feeling choices; TTS.
designs.distinctiveness: This is a comprehension-of-feelings task (RL describe characters' feelings) — no template reads a social scene to identify emotion; story-maker authors a story, this INTERPRETS one. Separation from #03/#10: those map need/clue to an item; this maps a narrated situation to an internal emotional state.
designs.asset_idea: stub: scene illustration placeholder + feeling-word/face buttons. CA5: emotive character art (happy/sad/left-out), small social scenes.

designs.name: Trade to Make Everyone Happy
designs.mechanic: Each friend HAS one item but WANTS another ('I have an apple, I want a banana'). The child taps two friends to TRADE so both get their wish — resolving a network of wants by one-to-one swaps until everyone's satisfied. Tie each satisfying swap to a quantity/decomposition the child verifies (K.OA.A.2 making a number two ways) so the swap-network instantiates a standard rather than being a relational puzzle.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each completed trade makes both friends cheer; the last swap turns the whole group's frowns to grins — 'everybody got what they wanted!'
designs.character_world: A friendly swap-market where friends trade snacks/toys.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — have/want graph; tap two characters, validate the swap satisfies both.
designs.distinctiveness: Unique trade/swap-resolution: it's a relational matching where you pair HAVE→WANT across characters (a directed-matching puzzle), distinct from #06 (static relationship pairs) because the correct swap depends on reciprocal want satisfaction. Separation from #14-style 'deliver': nothing is delivered from a tray; goods circulate among characters.
designs.asset_idea: stub: characters with have-bubble + want-bubble. CA5: market-stall friends, tradeable item sprites (apple, banana, ball).

designs.name: Tidy the Toy Shelf (Sort, Then Sort Again)
designs.mechanic: A messy pile must be organized into a shelf with rows AND columns: first by a major category (rows), then by a sub-attribute within each row (columns, e.g. by color or size). Correct placement requires satisfying TWO classification rules at once — the grid arrangement encodes a two-level organization. Make both row-rule and column-rule categorizable attributes the child names (classify into categories, K.MD.B.3) and count each cell, so cross-classification instantiates the data standard.
designs.fun_no_competition: Turning chaos into a perfectly organized display where everything matches its neighbors row and column; the shelf sparkles and the toys settle in contentedly.
designs.character_world: A tidy shopkeeper raccoon whose toy shelf got tumbled and who loves things grouped just so.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — 2D grid drop targets; check row-attr + col-attr on drop. Modest item count.
designs.distinctiveness: Sort-home is single-rule binning; this requires nested category-AND-subcategory placement, so a cell is correct only if BOTH its row-rule and column-rule hold. Separation: two-attribute cross-classification vs one-attribute binning.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 3x3 grid + colored category icons. CA5: raccoon shopkeeper, wooden shelf, toy objects in 3 categories × 3 colors, tidy-sparkle.

designs.name: Pack the Suitcase
designs.mechanic: A suitcase grid must be filled with packing items so they fit edge-to-edge with NO gaps and NO overlaps (a tetromino-style spatial pack). The child drags and rotates items so the arrangement exactly tiles the space. The completed packing IS the answer — composing shapes to fill a region.
designs.fun_no_competition: The satisfying click of the last piece filling the final gap and the lid snapping shut; everything fits perfectly, ready for the trip.
designs.character_world: A traveling hedgehog packing for a holiday who needs everything to fit so the suitcase will close.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — grid-snap drag with rotation; occupancy-map check for gaps/overlaps. Keep piece set small for K-3.
designs.distinctiveness: No template packs/tiles a bounded space. Closest is reveal-grid, but that uncovers cells; here the child PLACES shapes that must interlock without gaps. Separation: spatial composition/tiling vs revealing.
designs.asset_idea: stub: outlined suitcase grid + colored block shapes. CA5: hedgehog traveler, open suitcase with fabric lining, clothes/toy items as soft puzzle shapes, lid-close + click.

designs.name: Fit the Tangram Picture
designs.mechanic: A target silhouette (a cat, a boat) must be filled exactly by arranging a small set of given shapes — sliding, rotating, and flipping them to compose the picture with no overlap and no gap. The completed arrangement of parts IS the answer (compose shapes to make a larger shape).
designs.fun_no_competition: The final triangle dropping in to reveal the whole picture — a quiet 'ta-da'; the silhouette fills with color and the animal it forms gives a little wink.
designs.character_world: A shape-wizard cat conjuring pictures out of magic geometry tiles.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: needs-richer-runtime — free rotation/flip + non-grid overlap detection is heavier than snap-grid; doable with constrained snap-angles (45°) and predefined slots to stay shell-feasible.
designs.distinctiveness: Distinct from Pack the Suitcase (04): packing fills a rectangular grid with axis-aligned blocks; this composes free-form geometric shapes (triangles/squares) into a recognizable FIGURE, requiring rotation/flip and shape-composition reasoning. Separation: compose-named-figure vs grid-pack.
designs.asset_idea: stub: gray silhouette + plain colored polygons. CA5: shape-wizard cat, glowing tangram tiles, target silhouettes (animals/boats), reveal sparkle + wink.

designs.name: The Alphabet Queue
designs.mechanic: Letter-characters mill about wanting to get in line for the ice-cream truck. The child drags each into a queue so they stand in alphabetical order (or so a small set of words queues alphabetically by first letter). The left-to-right queue order encodes alphabetical sequencing.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each letter cheers 'my turn!' as it slots into the right spot; when the whole queue is correct they do a little wave down the line and the truck dings.
designs.character_world: Chatty letter-friends waiting politely in line for an ice-cream truck that only serves them in ABC order.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — drag-reorder list; alphabetical index comparison for lock. TTS can name each letter.
designs.distinctiveness: An ELA ordering core. Distinct from organize-order-01/02 (numeric/measured order) because the ordering key is the alphabet (symbolic sequence the child must KNOW, not compare perceptually). Distinct from sort-home (no bins) and match-pairs (no pairing).
designs.asset_idea: stub: lettered chips in a row. CA5: 26 expressive letter-characters (idle/excited), ice-cream truck, sidewalk queue, ABC arch sign.

designs.name: Fill the Ten-Frame Just Right
designs.mechanic: An empty ten-frame (two rows of five) must be filled with counters to show a target number, placed in the conventional order (fill the top row left-to-right first). The arrangement of counters within the frame's structured cells encodes the number's composition (e.g. 7 = a full five + two).
designs.fun_no_competition: Counters dropping into their cells with a soft pop, the frame filling row-by-row neatly; a satisfying 'full row' shimmer when the top five complete.
designs.character_world: An egg-carton-loving hen who fills her ten-frame nest with eggs, one tidy row at a time.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — fixed 2×5 grid; tap-to-fill in order; count check. Trivial runtime.
designs.distinctiveness: Distinct from organize-order-01 (a linear number line) — this is a STRUCTURED 5+5 frame where placement order and grouping reveal subitizing structure. Closest neighbor is the number line; separation is bounded 2-row composition vs unbounded ordinal line.
designs.asset_idea: stub: 2×5 outlined cells + dot counters. CA5: hen character, egg-carton ten-frame, eggs as counters, row-complete shimmer.

designs.name: Chronological: What Came First?
designs.mechanic: Picture-cards of life-stages or a day's routine (seed→sprout→tree, or morning→noon→night) sit shuffled. The child arranges them on a timeline track so they go earliest→latest. The timeline position encodes real-world temporal/causal order.
designs.fun_no_competition: Watching a tiny life-cycle bloom in order — the seed grows into a tree as the cards lock in; a calm, wholesome 'time passing' animation rewards the right order.
designs.character_world: A gentle gardener mole arranging photo-memories of how things grow, from first to last.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — drag-reorder onto a timeline; index vs canonical; short grow animation on success.
designs.distinctiveness: Distinct from Story-in-Order (07), which sequences a fictional narrative's events — this orders REAL-WORLD chronology/lifecycle as informational sequencing. Separation: informational time-order vs narrative plot-order.
designs.asset_idea: stub: photo-card placeholders on a line. CA5: gardener mole, timeline ribbon, life-cycle/routine illustration sets, sunrise-to-sunset color wash, grow playback.

designs.name: Sort the Coins Into the Right Tubes
designs.mechanic: Mixed coins (or place-value tokens: ones, tens, hundreds) tumble out; the child drags each into the matching labeled tube AND the tubes must end stacked in value order. Combines category placement with an ordered arrangement so the lineup of tubes reads least→greatest value.
designs.fun_no_competition: Coins clinking down into their tubes, the tubes filling like a chart; when all are sorted and value-ordered the piggy bank does a happy jingle.
designs.character_world: A thrifty piggy-bank pig organizing the day's coins into neat value tubes.
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — labeled tube drop-zones + value-order check on the tube row; counts shown as stacks.
designs.distinctiveness: Hybrid that is still distinct: sort-home only bins; here after binning, the BINS themselves must be value-ordered and the within-tube stack reveals quantity. Closest is Tidy Toy Shelf (06) but that's two perceptual attributes; this couples categorization with numeric value ordering and place value.
designs.asset_idea: stub: labeled tubes + token circles. CA5: piggy-bank pig, clear coin tubes (ones/tens/hundreds), coins/base-ten blocks, jingle + chart-fill animation.

designs.name: Rube-Goldberg Trigger Builder
designs.mechanic: A scene has 3 broken gaps in a chain (a missing ramp, a missing bucket, a missing fan). The child drags the correct piece into each gap from a tray, ORDERED first-to-last as the prompt narrates ('first the ball rolls, next it...'). Once all gaps are filled correctly, tapping GO runs the whole contraption. Anchor the first/next/last chain to retelling/sequencing a story's events (RL.K.2 / order events) with text, so building the chain instantiates sequencing rather than touching it.
designs.fun_no_competition: The full contraption fires in a chain — ball rolls, fan blows, balloon pops confetti — watching your assembled sequence run end-to-end is the joy.
designs.character_world: A bumbling cat-engineer's invention to wake a snoozing hamster
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — DOM gap slots + CSS sequential trigger animation chain
designs.distinctiveness: Multi-step cause-effect CHAIN where the child completes a sequence of triggers — distinct from domino-03 (homogeneous count) because each piece is a DIFFERENT mechanism and ORDER/role matters. Sequencing is the skill (first/next/last).
designs.asset_idea: stub: ramp/bucket/fan pieces + scene. CA5: per-mechanism action frames, final confetti pop, cat-engineer reactions

designs.name: Seed-to-Bloom Time Crank
designs.mechanic: A seed sits in soil with a time-crank handle. The child turns the crank and watches the plant grow through ordered stages (seed -> sprout -> bud -> bloom). The prompt names a stage and the child cranks to exactly that stage. Over-cranking wilts it (and they can crank back), teaching the ordered sequence. Require reading/ordering the first-next-last stage labels and setting to a named stage (RI.1.3 connect events/steps), so the dial instantiates the informational-sequence standard.
designs.fun_no_competition: Cranking the handle and watching the plant unfurl leaf by leaf, then bloom — and rewinding it back to a seed — is pure transform wonder.
designs.character_world: A gentle bug-gardener narrating its plant's growth
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — DOM crank slider + CSS stage crossfade
designs.distinctiveness: A reversible ORDERED-STAGE transform via a crank, focused on sequence/ordinal language. Distinct from melt-meter-05 (physical states of one substance) — this is biological GROWTH stages and targets ordinal sequencing. Closest neighbor melt-meter; separation: grow-stages teach first/next/last ordering, melt teaches states.
designs.asset_idea: stub: soil + crank + plant stages. CA5: seed->sprout->bud->bloom sequence + wilt frame, bug-gardener sprites

designs.name: Weather Machine Cause-Effect
designs.mechanic: A control panel has cause buttons (Sun, Rain, Wind, Cold). A scene shows a plant/puddle/snowman. The prompt states a desired EFFECT ('make the puddle disappear') and the child must press the cause that produces it (Sun -> puddle evaporates). Pressing the wrong cause shows a silly mismatch and asks again.
designs.fun_no_competition: Press Rain and a flower blooms; press Cold and the puddle freezes solid — the immediate transform reaction is the whole fun.
designs.character_world: A friendly cloud-creature operating a backyard weather console
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — DOM buttons + CSS scene-state swaps + sprite reactions
designs.distinctiveness: Pure cause->effect reasoning: pick the input that yields the stated outcome. Distinct from melt-meter-05 (one dial, one substance through states) because here multiple DIFFERENT causes map to different effects on different objects. Closest neighbor rube-goldberg-08; separation: that orders a chain, this is single cause->effect matching.
designs.asset_idea: stub: weather buttons + scene objects. CA5: per-effect transform sequences (bloom, evaporate, freeze, blow), cloud-creature sprites

designs.name: Word Plus-S Machine
designs.mechanic: A single object (one cat) goes in a conveyor. The child sees the word 'cat' and the prompt makes MORE of them (3 cats appear). The child must transform the word by adding the right ending — tapping the '+s' stamp to make 'cats' — and the machine only releases the correct plural that matches the picture count.
designs.fun_no_competition: The +s stamp THUNKS down and an extra letter pops on with a sparkle, then the right number of critters tumble out — the matching morph delights.
designs.character_world: A copy-machine factory run by a tidy raccoon who stamps words
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — DOM letter tiles + stamp animation + critter sprites
designs.distinctiveness: A WORD transform (singular->plural) triggered by a stamp, with the picture-count as the cause. Distinct from story-maker (assembling sentences) — here one word morphs by an inflection rule. Closest neighbor word-morph-13; separation: that swaps letters to make a new word, this appends a grammatical ending matched to quantity.
designs.asset_idea: stub: word tiles + +s stamp + critter PNGs. CA5: stamp thunk frames, sparkle on new letter, raccoon operator sprites

designs.name: Letter-Swap Morph Lab
designs.mechanic: A word sits in a chamber (cat). The prompt says 'change one sound to make CAP' or 'swap the first letter to make HAT'. The child drags the new letter into the right slot; the machine zaps and the word MORPHS, then a picture of the new word appears. One-letter-at-a-time transformation chains words.
designs.fun_no_competition: The zap, the letter spinning into place, and the picture flipping from a cat to a hat — watching one swap morph the whole word is magic.
designs.character_world: A word-wizard owl in a glowing transformation chamber
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — DOM letter slots + CSS zap + picture swap
designs.distinctiveness: A WORD-CHAIN transform: change one phoneme/letter to morph into a new word, with each step a real word. Distinct from plus-s-07 (append a grammatical ending) because here you SWAP a sound within the word (phonemic substitution). Distinct from build-a-word entirely — the chamber transforms an existing word.
designs.asset_idea: stub: word chamber + letter tiles + result pictures. CA5: zap morph frames, picture cross-swap, owl-wizard sprites

designs.name: Shape-Fold Transformer
designs.mechanic: A flat 2D shape (square, triangle pattern) sits on a folding table. The prompt asks 'fold this to make a cube/cone'. The child taps fold lines in sequence and the net animates folding up into the 3D shape. Choosing the right net + folds transforms flat into solid with a snap.
designs.fun_no_competition: The flat paper creases and lifts into a real cube with a crisp snap — watching 2D pop into 3D is a tiny delightful miracle.
designs.character_world: An origami-fox who folds flat scraps into pop-up creatures
designs.web_shell_feasibility: needs-richer-runtime — true 3D fold animation is hard in pure DOM/CSS; feasible with pre-rendered CA5 fold sprite-sheets per net rather than live 3D
designs.distinctiveness: A geometric 2D->3D transform via folding — the cause (which folds) produces the solid. Distinct from marble-branch-09 (route logic) — this morphs a flat net into a named solid. Closest neighbor letter-swap-13 (a chamber morph) but operates on SHAPES not words and teaches 2D/3D relationships.
designs.asset_idea: stub: flat net + fold-line buttons + solid result. CA5: per-net fold-up sequence sprite-sheets, snap pop, origami-fox sprites

designs.name: Recipe Double & Half
designs.mechanic: A recipe lists ingredient amounts for 2 cupcakes. A sign flips to 'Make 4!' (double) or 'Make 1!' (half). The child taps each ingredient up or down to the correct doubled/halved amount, then the oven bakes — correct amounts yield perfect cupcakes, wrong yields a lopsided one. Drop the 6.RP ratio framing; restrict to doubling/halving small whole quantities as repeated addition of equal groups (2.OA.C.4), so it stays a K-3 equal-groups task, not proportional reasoning.
designs.fun_no_competition: The oven dings and reveals a tray of identical perfect cupcakes (or one comically melted one) — predicting the bake outcome is the joy.
designs.character_world: A bakery run by a tiny mouse chef who narrates each bake with delight
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — DOM steppers + oven sprite reveal
designs.distinctiveness: Not magic-machine's one-op-one-output: this transforms an ENTIRE SET of quantities by the same scalar (doubling/halving each line). Closest neighbor potion-ratio-01; separation: ratio-lab matches a proportion in one batch, this applies x2 or /2 to every ingredient simultaneously (operate, not match).
designs.asset_idea: stub: ingredient icons + number steppers. CA5: oven door open/close, perfect cupcake tray + lopsided fail variant, mouse-chef cheer/oops sprites

designs.name: Caption the Photo (All-About Frame)
designs.mechanic: An informational photo (a frog, a fire truck) sits above a 'topic + 2 facts' frame. The child taps the photo's topic word into the topic slot, then drags two true fact-cards (from a tray mixing true facts and off-topic/false ones) into the two fact slots, producing a tiny 'All About ___' caption the page reads back. The frame only completes when the topic names the picture AND both facts are true of it.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each true fact dragged in makes a little fact-firefly land and glow on the caption card; when the All-About card is whole, a friendly owl 'reads' it aloud and stamps a paper-clip badge. No timer — swap facts and rebuild your caption as many times as you like.
designs.character_world: Professor Hoot the owl running a cozy nature-notebook studio
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — slots are drop-zones; true/false fact cards carry a data-flag checked on drop; TTS read-back of assembled string. No game loop.
designs.distinctiveness: All the existing sentence work (C031 opinion-scaffold, C007 cloze, C036 compound) is single-sentence or word-level. This produces a structured INFORMATIVE text (topic statement + supplied facts) — the W.K.2/W.1.2 shape — by selecting true facts about a pictured topic. Not opinion (C031), not comprehension Q&A (C092).
designs.asset_idea: stub: photo + gray slot rectangles + plain fact cards; CA5 art: hand-painted notebook page, fact-firefly sprite, Professor Hoot read/stamp sprite-sheet

designs.name: Tell the Story in Pictures (Narrative Builder)
designs.mechanic: Three empty story-frames labeled First / Next / Last sit on an easel. The child drags character + setting + action stickers into each frame to STAGE a tiny three-beat narrative, then taps a 'time-word' chip (First, Then, Finally) onto each frame. The story is accepted when each frame is non-empty, the actions form a sensible order the child chose, and each frame carries its sequence word — producing a narrated beginning-middle-end.
designs.fun_no_competition: When all three frames are staged and labeled, a tiny puppet theater curtain sweeps and the three scenes play left-to-right with a gentle chime as each time-word lights. No score — restage the whole story freely.
designs.character_world: Mim the mouse stage-director in a paper puppet theater
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — three drop-frames + sticker palette + sequence-word chips; acceptance = all-frames-filled + each has a time-word. Curtain/playback is a CSS sprite sequence, no physics.
designs.distinctiveness: C097 RETELLS a given story; C144 orders given informational cards. This one has the child PRODUCE an original narrative by staging three beats and labeling them with temporal words — the W.K.3/W.1.3 narrative-writing shape (recount events in order, use temporal words). Generative, not reconstructive.
designs.asset_idea: stub: three boxes + emoji-ish stickers; CA5 art: paper puppet stage, character/setting/action sticker set, Mim director sprite-sheet

designs.name: Two Reasons Why (Opinion + Because)
designs.mechanic: A topic card poses a choice ('Which pet is best?'). The child taps their opinion chip ('I think dogs are best'), then must drag exactly TWO 'because' reason-cards from a tray that actually support that opinion (true-of-dogs supports vs off-topic distractors) into two because-slots, building 'I think ___ because ___ and ___.' The opinion sentence completes only with a stated opinion plus two relevant linked reasons.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each well-matched reason makes a vine grow another leaf up a trellis toward the opinion-flower; two good reasons bloom it open. Off-topic cards gently spring back with a soft 'hmm'. Rebuild your argument as often as you like.
designs.character_world: Bea the bee tending an opinion-garden trellis
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — opinion chip + two because drop-slots; reason-cards carry supports-flag for the chosen opinion. Trellis grow = CSS height transitions.
designs.distinctiveness: C031 builds a single opinion/declarative sentence; this extends to the grade-2 opinion shape (W.2.1: state an opinion + supply REASONS + use linking word 'because/and'). The relevance gate on the reason-cards is the distinct cognitive move.
designs.asset_idea: stub: opinion chip + slots + plain cards; CA5 art: garden trellis, opinion-flower bloom frames, Bea sprite-sheet

designs.name: Show-and-Tell Circle (Take-Turns Talk)
designs.mechanic: A circle of puppet friends passes a 'talking feather'. On the child's turn a prompt appears ('Tell one thing about your picture'); the child taps the sentence-tile sequence that makes a COMPLETE on-topic spoken turn, then must tap 'pass the feather' — and on others' turns must wait (the pass-button is disabled while a friend speaks) and then tap the chip that BUILDS ON what the last friend said (same topic). Models one-speaker-at-a-time, stay-on-topic, build-on-others.
designs.fun_no_competition: The talking feather glows and floats to each friend in turn; a small 'listening ear' lights above the friend who is speaking so you know to wait. Taking your turn and building on a friend makes both puppets nod warmly. No clock — the circle goes around as gently as you want.
designs.character_world: A ring of cozy classroom puppets sharing on a story rug
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — turn-state machine (whose turn, pass disabled while speaking), sentence-tile assembly, build-on check = shared-topic flag. All DOM state, no loop.
designs.distinctiveness: C093 is choose-a-polite-line two-way improv; C095 parses a compound request. None model the COLLABORATIVE-CONVERSATION RULES of SL.K.1/SL.1.1/SL.2.1 (take turns, one at a time, build on others, stay on topic). The waiting + build-on-the-last-turn mechanic is the instantiation.
designs.asset_idea: stub: circle of colored dots + feather icon; CA5 art: puppet friends on a rug, glowing feather, listening-ear glow, nod animations

designs.name: Ask the Right Question (Clarify the Mystery Box)
designs.mechanic: A friend holds a covered box and says 'I have something inside'. The child must PRODUCE clarifying questions by assembling question-word + frame tiles ('What ... is it?', 'How many ... ?', 'Where ... ?'). Each well-formed, relevant question the friend answers with a clue; the child asks until they can name the hidden thing. The skill is generating the question (ask-to-clarify), not answering one.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each good question makes the box rattle and a clue-bubble pop with a soft pop sound; the cover turns gradually see-through as you learn more. Naming the thing lifts the lid with a happy reveal. No penalties for an off-target question — the friend just says 'I'm not sure how to answer that, try another!'
designs.character_world: Gus the gopher guarding a curious wrapped box
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — question-tile assembler validates question-word + frame; each valid+relevant question maps to a stored clue; reveal = opacity transition. No loop.
designs.distinctiveness: C071 narrows from clues the GAME gives; here the child PRODUCES the questions (SL.K.3/SL.1.3 ask and answer questions to seek help / get info / clarify). Generative question-asking with question-word grammar is absent from the 152.
designs.asset_idea: stub: box + question-word tiles; CA5 art: wrapped mystery box, clue-bubble pops, Gus gopher sprite-sheet

designs.name: What's It Mostly About? (Main-Idea Net)
designs.mechanic: A short illustrated informational paragraph (3-4 sentences, read aloud) appears with four 'idea-fish' swimming below — three are small supporting details, one is the big main topic. The child casts a net over the ONE main-idea fish (the umbrella the others fit under), then drags the three detail-fish under it to show they belong to it. Correct only when the chosen idea is the topic AND the details nest beneath it.
designs.fun_no_competition: The main-idea fish glows golden and grows a little umbrella; the detail-fish swim into a happy school beneath it with bubbly chimes. A wrong cast just lets that fish wriggle free with a giggle. Re-read and recast freely.
designs.character_world: Nila the otter fishing for ideas in a calm reading-pond
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — paragraph TTS + four tappable fish (one flagged main); net = tap-select; nesting = drop-zone under the chosen fish. Bubble/glow are CSS.
designs.distinctiveness: C059 reads a diagram's labels for a specific function; C092/C094 are RL recall/feeling. None target MAIN-IDEA-vs-detail (RI.K.2/RI.1.2/RI.2.2: identify the main topic and retell key details). The detail-nesting move makes the topic/detail hierarchy explicit.
designs.asset_idea: stub: text + four labeled circles; CA5 art: reading-pond, idea-fish with umbrella, Nila otter sprite-sheet

designs.name: Why Did the Author Tell Me? (Purpose Sorter)
designs.mechanic: Short text snippets (a recipe step, a funny rhyme, a 'fact about bats') float in one at a time. The child sorts each into one of three labeled author-intent bins: 'to TELL me facts', 'to make me LAUGH/enjoy', 'to teach me HOW to do it'. The bin glows when the snippet's purpose matches; a why-chip then asks the child to confirm the textual cue that signals it.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each snippet sails into its bin on a little paper airplane; the matching bin puffs a colored confetti-poof matching its purpose (fact=blue, fun=pink, how-to=green). No streak counter — sort and re-sort as you read.
designs.character_world: Edda the editor-elephant sorting the morning mail at a tiny post office
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — snippet cards carry a purpose-flag; three drop-bins; confirm-cue is a second tap on the signaling phrase. All DOM.
designs.distinctiveness: Existing sorts classify by perceptual/phonological/category attributes (C018, C075, C139). None sort by AUTHOR'S PURPOSE/text-type (RI.2.6 identify the main purpose; RI.K.6/RI.1.6 role of author; RL.K.5 text types). Purpose-as-the-sorting-rule is a new comprehension axis.
designs.asset_idea: stub: text cards + three labeled bins; CA5 art: post office, paper-airplane snippets, Edda elephant sprite-sheet

designs.name: Beginning, Middle, End Spine (Story Structure)
designs.mechanic: A heard story plays; below it a 'story spine' has three labeled bone-segments: Beginning (who/where), Middle (the problem), End (how it was solved). The child drags the one event-card that fills each STRUCTURAL role — not just time order, but the right KIND of event (a setting card can't go in the 'problem' slot). The spine clicks together only when each role-card matches its structural function.
designs.fun_no_competition: Each correctly-placed role-card snaps onto the dino spine with a satisfying click; completing the spine makes a friendly story-dragon stretch and the whole tale replay along its back. Mis-typed cards wobble off gently. Rebuild freely.
designs.character_world: Dot the story-dragon whose back IS the story spine
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — three role-slots with type-tags; event-cards carry a role-type; match on drop. Replay-along-the-spine is a CSS sprite walk.
designs.distinctiveness: C097 retells in time order; C144 orders real-world chronology. This targets STORY STRUCTURE/elements (RL.K.5/RL.1.5 recognize text structure; identify setting/problem/solution roles) — the cards are matched to a narrative FUNCTION, not merely sequenced. The role-typing is the distinct demand.
designs.asset_idea: stub: three labeled segments + plain cards; CA5 art: dragon spine, story-event cards, Dot dragon sprite-sheet

designs.name: Whose Eyes? (Point of View Telescope)
designs.mechanic: A short scene is shown with two characters. A telescope can be pointed at either character; looking through it shows the scene 'from their eyes' (what they can see / how they'd describe it). The child reads a first-person line ('I was scared of the big wave') and aims the telescope at the character WHO is telling it / whose view it is, then taps the matching feeling-thought-bubble.
designs.fun_no_competition: Aiming the telescope tints the scene in that character's color and floats their thought-bubble; landing on the right speaker makes the lens sparkle and the character wave. No timer — sweep the telescope between characters as much as you like.
designs.character_world: Pim the penguin lighthouse-keeper with a story-telescope
designs.web_shell_feasibility: feasible — telescope = pointer-select over two characters; each speaker line maps to a character flag; tint/bubble are CSS overlays. No loop.
designs.distinctiveness: C094 reads a line's feeling/tone; C092 recalls details. None address POINT OF VIEW / who is telling the story (RL.K.6/RL.1.6/RL.2.6 identify who is telling at points in a story). The perspective-swap telescope makes 'whose view' the explicit task.
designs.asset_idea: stub: two character silhouettes + telescope icon; CA5 art: lighthouse balcony, perspective-tinted scenes, Pim penguin sprite-sheet

designs.name: Two Tales, One Difference (Compare Stories)
designs.mechanic: Two short illustrated story-strips about similar characters (two different 'lost mitten' tales) play side by side. The child is asked a compare question ('In which story does the mitten get found?') and taps the correct story-strip, then drags a 'same' card and a 'different' card to the elements that match vs differ across the two (same: both lose a mitten; different: who finds it). Builds same/different comparison across two texts.
